articles.title: Defense Without Limits
articles.body:
Defense Without Limits
Iranian officials say Tehran will place no limits on hitting aggressors and their regional backers in case of a renewed US-Israeli attack
TEHRAN – The tone of the enemy toward Iran has sharply escalated again, with senior American and Israeli officials openly speaking of finishing the job and some analysts warning a new round of war is near, while Iranian political and military officials say the country is fully ready for a severe and unrestricted response.
An informed Iranian source told Press TV that Iran has prepared for an all-out, multi-layered and comprehensive war. According to the source, Tehran has made a firm decision that in reaction to any aggression, assassination and terror, it will respond without any limitation or restraint and will crush with full force the accessible interests and targets of the aggressors and their supporters in the region.
From Tehran's point of view, the source said, the US will not launch an attack without Israel, nor Israel without the US, and talk of their independence from each other in a war against Iran resembles a bitter joke. The explicit threats by American officials and the Zionist regime to attack Iran, the source added, have provided the legal and moral license for Iran to adopt necessary defensive measures.
"We will soon finish the job"
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Iran had been "systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially, and unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job."
In the same post, Trump gave his "complete and total endorsement" to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 parliamentary election, suggesting Washington could take on the fight itself if Netanyahu failed to stay in power: with the "wrong Leader" in Israel, "America will have to do this work ourselves."
Trump did not specify what action he had in mind. Earlier this month he had said the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 US midterm elections and had spoken of "productive discussions." His latest comments came after he and Netanyahu discussed a possible new military operation, according to Axios, which reported last week that Netanyahu raised intelligence suggesting Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear program. Trump has also raised the possibility of striking the underground Pickaxe Mountain complex near Natanz.
At a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, Trump said the US was in a position to walk away from the war now, describing Iran as devastated and adding: "They're not going to have a nuclear weapon."
Netanyahu matched the tone. In a briefing with Israeli journalists on Sunday, he declared that bringing down the Islamic Republic remained a key objective and that he had directed all security agencies to pursue it: "We must bring this regime down once and for all."
Presenting an updated security doctrine, he said, as reported by Israel Hayom: "The objectives I set do not depend on American approval. To the extent necessary, we will also act independently. We have done so before, and if necessary, we will do so again. We are prepared to take the initiative. We must prevent the enemy from delivering the first blow."
He described confronting Iran as his "life's mission," claimed "90% of the job is done" by pointing to economic pressure and protests, and responded to Trump's endorsement with: "Together we will complete the mission!" In a video of a phone call released Monday, he told Trump: "Donald, we have a job to finish, you said it, and we'll finish it together."
In an interview with Fox News on October 18, Netanyahu warned Iran is developing intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching US cities and seeking nuclear warheads, saying: "You are the real target." He listed as his first priority if reelected: "First, we will achieve the complete elimination of the Iranian threat to Israel, to America, and to the entire world."
Unannounced visit and election countdown
The rhetoric moved with military signals. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth paid an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, October 19, meeting Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz at Ovda Air Base in the Negev. Spokesman Doron Spielman said they discussed "the threats in the region" and offensive-defensive cooperation. The Pentagon gave no details.
On Tuesday, Hegseth told US troops in the Central Command area: "I got to see some of our warfighters — they're preparing and ready to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon," adding they were "ready to go."
Israel canceled soldiers' leave from Thursday ahead of the vote. Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir said forces were on "a high level of alertness and readiness" against "external interference." Netanyahu told i24NEWS on Tuesday that Iran and its proxies could try to disrupt the October 27 election.
"Either a deal or an attack"
The Financial Times reported on Wednesday, October 21, citing a person familiar with Israeli planning, that renewed US-Israeli strikes in the coming weeks are "not an unreasonable scenario." Three sources said Netanyahu urged the military earlier this month to prepare a multi-day offensive including nuclear sites, planned for the weekend of October 10, which did not proceed after Trump opposed action before the US midterms. One source said: "There will either be a deal or an attack."
White House deputy spokesperson Anna Kelly told the FT the US "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections." The New York Times quoted Raz Zimmt of Tel Aviv's INSS as saying: "The baseline expectation in Iran, and in Israel, is that it's a matter of when the war restarts, not if." He added a strike alone would likely not achieve Washington's goals but might give Trump "an image of victory and a way out."
Ready for war, ready for diplomacy
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iraq's Al-Ekhbariya chanel that Iran entered three rounds of talks and all three led to war. "We were in the midst of negotiations and in the end it was proven that the Americans cannot be trusted. In the third round, we reached an understanding with Trump, but Trump himself violated it and adhered to it for only two weeks."
After more than eight months, Washington has achieved none of its objectives, he said, calling that a strategic failure for the US and a strategic success for Iran. America is now in a deep quagmire, resorting to military threats, sanctions and pressure on neighbors not to cooperate with Tehran, without result. "Iran will never surrender, neither to sanctions nor to military threats. The only solution is diplomacy and a negotiated solution."
"Every possibility exists, including that the Americans and the Zionist regime will start another war. But we are in full readiness. We are fully prepared to defend ourselves and will stand until the last moment," Araghchi said. "When I say we are ready for war, it does not mean we want war. It is a message to do calculations and not enter that war again. We are as ready for diplomacy as we are for war."
The main deterrent, he argued, is that readiness: Americans know war cannot deliver their goals. In the two wars, they "fell into Israel's trap, more precisely Netanyahu's trap. Netanyahu will do anything for his personal goal, not for America, Israel or anyone else."
In a Financial Times essay titled "The false assumptions about us are dangerous," Araghchi wrote that a way forward requires Washington to accept it has "no military options." Trump entered the war on "fundamentally erroneous assumptions," being wrongly told Iranian forces are unprepared, despite lessons learned since 2025. "In June 2025 and February 2026, they bombed us while we were negotiating. And in June this year, shortly after an agreement was signed by Presidents Pezeshkian and Trump, we were attacked a third time. How can we trust a US president again?"
He recalled presenting a Seven-Day Plan via mediators at the UN General Assembly under which the US would do nothing it had not already agreed to: the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on Day 6, talks for a final deal on Day 7. He cited Moody's that the war has cost US consumers $265 billion this year, about $2,000 per household, half from energy prices, plus damaged bases and equipment losses. Further escalation, he warned, would put civilian lives, regional states and the world economy at great risk and bring "even greater strategic failure."
Defense without restraint
Armed Forces General Staff spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi replied to Trump and Netanyahu: "We tell the child-killing twins, Trump and Netanyahu: you are on the slope of decline, and with boasting you will not save yourselves from the swamp of death."
New Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, approved Sunday with 237 votes, wrote he devoted his first working hour to the IRGC Aerospace Force and Army air defense: "For us, responding to threats is not a rhetorical contest; it is turning threats into greater readiness. We are focused on our targets with new technologies; we eat dust but we will not give away soil."
National Security Commission Chairman Ebrahim Azizi wrote on X: "Regardless of your election results, we have no doubt about your hostility. We are ready, in response to any operational mistake, to wipe you off the map."
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei wrote Wednesday on X, reacting to the US Secretary of State's call to condemn Iran over Persian Gulf insecurity: "In less than nine months, they attacked Iran twice in the middle of negotiations; they slaughtered our children in Minab, killed our daughters in Lamard, assassinated our leaders, and intensified sanctions; and now, after blatantly violating the understanding they signed, while claiming victory, they ask the world to condemn Iran." The world, he said, is paying for US-Israeli law-breaking, from regional turmoil to energy insecurity. "You cannot set fires, throw the region into chaos, then stand as plaintiff and ask others to condemn the victim."
Ball in Washington's court
Tehran sees a deadlock not easily broken. The gap over the balance of conflict, US pressure to force submission before the midterms, Iran's tighter control of Hormuz and action against violating vessels, oil above $110 after two tankers carrying 4 million barrels hit mines — one burning, one halted — the criticized diesel deal with Russia, and Hegseth's secret talks with Netanyahu alongside UAE officials all point to continued tension.
 
While unofficial sources speak of a Pakistan-Qatar proposal, Tehran believes Trump seeks to pass the midterms, not end a costly war whose declared goals keep changing. Iran does not doubt Islamabad's sincerity, but the ball, officials say, is in Washington's court. Until the US abandons the illusion of forcing surrender and imposing unilateral terms, by negotiation or aggression, the conflict will not end.

articles.title: Race to halt US-Iran escalation as attacks on shipping intensify
articles.body:
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
Breadcrumb
Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Middle East. Here is the latest:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a peace deal with Iran would be "extremely difficult" to achieve unless Tehran stops attacking ships in Hormuz. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, meanwhile, said that while Iran was "firmly committed to seeking a dignified peaceful resolution to the conflict, we are also fully prepared to defend ourselves".
In Yemen, a ballistic missile targeted Aden International Airport on Wednesday - the third such attack this month amid escalating strikes with Saudi Arabia and a tightening siege on Taizz.
Israeli attacks continue in Gaza, the West Bank, southern Lebanon and Syria.
The US is reportedly repositioning troops and evacuating some diplomats in Middle East ahead of possible escalation of region's wars, according to NBC and other reports, citing unidentified officials.
A Tunisian court on Wednesday sentenced 10 environmental activists to up to a year in prison over an anti-pollution protest they attended in 2020, a defence lawyer said.
Eight of them were sentenced to six-month suspended sentences, lawyer Hamida Chaieb said.
The activists had taken part in a demonstration against a major phosphate-processing factory in southern Tunisia's coastal city of Gabes, where locals have complained about pollution and health issues they linked to the plant.
The case stemmed from a complaint by the state-run factory, which accused the activists of obstructing its operations, Chaieb said.
The activists were arrested at the time but later released amid pressure from rights groups.
Read the full story here.
An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in eastern Saudi Arabia's Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Egypt rejected on Wednesday Libya's eastern-based parliament's ratification of a long-disputed maritime agreement with Turkey, saying it infringed on Cairo's rights in the Mediterranean.
The agreement "constitutes a clear infringement upon Egypt's sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone and continental shelf", Egypt's foreign ministry said.
Cairo said the agreement violates the Law of the Sea, and was therefore "null and void, possesses no legal effect, and its ratification by the Libyan House of Representatives carries no legal consequences for Egypt".
An Austrian woman and a Swiss woman arrived in the eastern Libyan city of Benghazi after being freed from more than 18 months of detention in Niger, two officials speaking on the condition of anonymity said on Wednesday.
The Austrian, identified by Austrian authorities as Eva G, who is in her 70s, was kidnapped in the desert town of Agadez in central Niger in January 2025. Little information has been released about which group was holding her or what demands they may have made. She had been living in Niger for years.
The Swiss woman was taken hostage in April 2025. The Swiss Foreign Ministry did not previously name the hostage.
The two officials said the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after the necessary procedures were completed. They added that the operation was overseen by Saddam Haftar, deputy commander-in-chief of Libya's armed forces.
Niger, like its neighbours Mali and Burkina Faso, is battling a jihadist insurgency linked to al Qaeda and Islamic State that spun out of a Tuareg rebellion in northern Mali in 2012. The fighting has killed thousands and displaced millions across West Africa's central Sahel region over the past decade.
Kidnappings appeared to intensify in Niger last year.
Lina Attalah, co-founder and editor-in-chief of independent news website Mada Masr, appeared for questioning on Wednesday after she was summoned by Egyptian authorities, who did not specify the reasons for the summons or the subject of the investigation.
The summons came after Mada Masr published a report detailing complaints by detainees who said they had been subjected to violations inside Egyptian prisons.
"Prosecutors have been investigating Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah for three hours at the headquarters of the Supreme State Security Prosecution in New Cairo. Her defence team has been present with her throughout the questioning. The investigation session is ongoing," Mada Masr wrote on X on Wednesday.
Iran's state media reported on Wednesday the sound of explosions in the southern Hormozgan province overlooking the Strait of Hormuz.
"A few minutes ago, the sound of several explosions was heard in the Karpan area of Sirik, in Hormozgan Province," the official IRNA news agency said, adding that "local sources have not yet disclosed the nature of these explosions."
Two people were killed in an attack on Saudi Arabia's Shaybah oilfield after air defences intercepted a drone attempting to target a facility at the field in the Eastern region, state news agency reported on Wednesday citing an energy ministry official.
There was no impact on operations in the field following the drone attack.
The US State Department is preparing to issue an ordered departure of some personnel and family members from US embassies across the Gulf region, three US officials said on Wednesday.
The move was due to a possible resumption of hostilities, particularly with Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen, two of the US officials said.
Explosions were heard in Sirik in southern Iran, Iranian media reported on Wednesday, adding the nature and origin of the explosions were unknown.
Israeli forces on Wednesday briefly detained a US congressional candidate as he joined activists supporting Palestinians harvesting olives in the face of threats by extremist settlers.
Brad Lander, a left-wing Democrat who is expected to easily win a House seat in New York City on November 3, posted on social media that he was detained along with a group of rabbis and volunteers as they harvested olives west of Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank.
"The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn't a crime under any law I know," Lander wrote on X.
He later wrote that he was released on account of his prominence, adding that "Palestinians face far worse consequences every day".
An Israeli airstrike has reportedly targeted Haddatha in southern Lebanon, according to state media on Wednesday evening.
There is no military solution to the civil war tearing Sudan apart, the United Nations envoy on the conflict insisted Wednesday following international talks on peace efforts.
A total of 21 countries and five international organisations gathered at the UN headquarters in Geneva for the so-called Sixth Consultative Meeting on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives and Efforts in Sudan.
The two warring parties were not represented.
The war between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, displaced more than 13 million and created the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.
Talks co-chair Pekka Haavisto, UN chief Antonio Guterres' personal envoy for Sudan, said the regular armed forces and the RSF still believed in a military victory in the war.
"We as the international community are saying that there is no military solution to the conflict in Sudan," the former Finnish foreign minister told a press conference after the talks concluded.
"The solution has to be found from diplomatic talks and discussions.
"One small step that the United Nations has been taking is trying to introduce so-called confidence-building measures: some steps that both parties can agree."
He said one was the possible exchange of prisoners of war or detainees -- both military and civilian -- and another was on facilitating student exams.
"We think that there are issues that should unite actually both parties of the conflict -- but these are, of course, baby steps compared with the terrible destruction that is happening," Haavisto admitted.
Yemeni media affiliated with Houthi militant group reports three women killed, three children injured following artillery shelling allegedly by Saudi-backed forces in Hadhran area near Taizz. Additional strikes were subsequently reported on Wednesday evening.
The US Treasury Department on Wednesday imposed sanctions on Panama and Greek-based law firm Karnakis and Karnakis, which it said has supported Iranian shipping for years.
The US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network also issued an administrative subpoena to advance an investigation into a Greek bank over potential ties to Iran, according to a Treasury statement, which did not name the bank.
FINCEN also issued requests for information to six other banks in Europe over relationships with Iranian financial institutions under US sanctions.
A Tunisian military court sentenced opposition politician Olfa Hamdi to four years in prison on charges of plotting against state security and inciting the military to disobey orders, her lawyer said on Wednesday, the latest move against opponents of President Kais Saied.
Hamdi, the leader of the Third Republic Party who holds US citizenship, was detained at Tunisia's main airport after disembarking from a flight in February.
She had been living abroad and previously served as CEO of Tunisia's national carrier Tunisair.
Hamdi has repeatedly criticized Saied’s rule and called for a transitional government and early presidential elections.
The sentence comprises two separate two-year prison terms and total fines of 80,000 dinars ($26,000), her lawyer Akram Moussa told Reuters. Hamdi was sentenced in March in a separate case to two years in prison.
Many opposition leaders, along with activists and journalists, are behind bars, with critics accusing Saied of having turned Tunisia into a prison since 2021.
Saied rejects the accusations, saying he is not a dictator and that the law applies to everyone, regardless of their position.
Azerbaijan on Wednesday barred 31 Turkish nationals, including an opposition lawmaker and party leaders, from entering the country, escalating a rare dispute between the close allies over restrictions on Islamic headscarves in schools.
Tensions flared after Azerbaijan introduced school uniform rules last month barring additions deemed incompatible with secular education.
Although the rules do not explicitly mention headscarves, girls wearing hijabs have reportedly been turned away from schools, sparking protests.
The foreign ministry in Baku said those blacklisted had used social media and online platforms to make statements "targeting the sovereignty, national security, constitutional order, people and leadership of the Republic of Azerbaijan."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday it intercepted six drones launched towards the kingdom, including in the Medina region home to one of Islam's holiest cities.
"Four drones launched towards the kingdom have been intercepted and destroyed," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X, adding in a second post that the interceptions took place in Saudi Arabia's Eastern province, as well as Medina.
Al-Malki, who did not specify who was behind the launches, later said another drone had been intercepted, also in the Eastern province.
On Wednesday evening, the coalition announced it had intercepted a sixth drone launched by the Houthis.
The Houthis earlier denied having targeted the kingdom, with military spokesman Yahya Saree saying their forces had not carried out any operations "deep" in Saudi territory.
Saudi forces renew their artillery shelling of border towns in Yemen's eastern Saada province, according to Houthi-affiliated media.
US Vice President JD Vance has refused to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of next week's elections, breaking with President Donald Trump amid growing divisions within the MAGA movement over Israel and Washington's involvement in Middle East conflicts.
Speaking to journalist Mark Halperin on Monday, Vance declined to follow Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu, who faces a difficult re-election battle on 27 October.
"I'm not anti-endorsing him. I'm not pro-endorsing him. I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections," Vance said.
"I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on the midterms," he added.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," state-linked media reported.
Al-Qahera News, which is closely linked to state intelligence and is to broadcast a speech by Sisi, reported that he also said "the stability of our brothers in the Gulf concerns Egypt's national security". The speech itself has not yet been aired.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult".
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
He added that Egypt has said it "will not enter Yemen or engage in a war against Yemen".
The decade-plus war between the Iran-backed Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government reignited in July.
The Houthis seized much of Yemen's Red Sea coastline in September and have since launched attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on state oil giant Aramco and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed on October 10.
Egypt's parliament on Monday delayed a debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia until next week.
Sisi had asked lawmakers to approve military support for Saudi Arabia if requested by the kingdom, which has come under near-daily attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Sisi said Egypt was not seeking to "confront or attack anyone", adding: "We are speaking only about defence."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that the the only way to remove the threat posed by Iran was to topple its government.
"Iran wanted to destroy us; we stopped them. They wanted to produce nuclear bombs; we stopped them... Yet they persist," he said during an election rally in the southern town of Dimona. "Therefore, there is only one way to end this: by toppling this regime."
"This is the directive I have issued to the Israel Defense Forces, to the Mossad, and to all our security branches," he added, without specifying when or how that directive would be executed.
Saudi Arabia has agreed to supply extra diesel to France "for as many months as necessary", the Elysee Palace told AFP on Wednesday, as President Emmanuel Macron was visiting Riyadh days after violent rioting across France.
Macron and de facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman met in Riyadh where they also agreed to consult on expanding security cooperation and infrastructure projects to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, the palace added.

articles.title: US Restores Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine as Witkoff Heads to Putin
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States had resumed sharing intelligence on Russian strikes with Kyiv, as US special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia for talks with President Vladimir Putin following a meeting with Zelensky in Norway.
Zelensky said on Tuesday that Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks, apparently restoring a service that the White House had suspended the previous week. He welcomed the resumption, saying it would help save lives.
“We are thankful that intelligence works,” Zelensky told reporters in Oslo, describing the warnings as “very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians” ahead of ballistic missile strikes.
Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg on Wednesday morning, Russian state news agency TASS reported. His visit is part of US President Donald Trump's efforts to ease a bitter dispute with Zelensky over how to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described Witkoff's discussions with Zelensky as positive and said the envoy would present their ideas to the Russian side. A US official told Reuters that Witkoff aimed to establish a route toward direct trilateral talks and broader multilateral negotiations. Axios reported that he would bring Putin an updated proposal for ending the war.
Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussions with Zelensky remotely and was also expected to participate virtually in the meeting with Putin, a US official told AFP. Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev was due to meet Witkoff at the airport before the talks.
The diplomatic efforts follow days of worsening relations between Washington and Kyiv. Trump has accused Zelensky of failing to pursue an end to the war and called for new Ukrainian leadership, while also criticizing Kyiv for refusing to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries.
On Tuesday, Trump again urged the Ukrainian president to agree to a deal with Moscow, saying Zelensky could have accepted terms offered during their contentious meeting in the Oval Office in February 2025.
“We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office,” Trump said.
Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard, an American captured by Russian forces in occupied Ukraine. It was unclear whether the request would be raised during Wednesday's meeting.
“I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens,” Trump told reporters in Washington.
The dispute escalated after Trump announced the lifting of US sanctions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He subsequently announced an energy ceasefire that Ukraine observed for several days, while Russia did not.
Washington's actions have fueled concern in Kyiv and among European and British supporters of Ukraine that the United States is increasingly favoring Moscow. US proposals for peace have largely reflected Russia's maximalist demands.
Zelensky said he had held a positive telephone conversation with Rubio earlier on Tuesday. Asked whether Ukraine was losing the war following recent US actions, he rejected the suggestion while acknowledging the cost of continued Russian attacks.
“Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It's a pity,” Zelensky said.
He also told Rubio about restrictions imposed the previous week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk's satellite internet service. The reported reduction in service speeds has hampered Ukraine's ability to conduct mid-range drone strikes against Russian battlefield positions.
Trump denied ordering the slowdown after Musk said the decision could only have come from the White House. Rubio said on Wednesday in Mumbai that Washington had not known in advance about the reduction in satellite communications speeds.
“The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk,” Rubio said.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown affecting the military-grade service.
Ukraine has also raised concerns over delays in the delivery of Patriot missile interceptors. Zelensky said he had offered to halt Ukraine's long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries, a key demand from Trump, if Washington supplied Kyiv with the interceptors.
The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriot systems purchased by other countries for Ukraine, leaving the country more exposed to Russian air attacks. Zelensky told US senators on Monday that missiles already paid for by European countries were being held up pending approval from US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Several European countries were prepared to transfer interceptors from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US authorization.
US officials have denied deliberately reducing support for Ukraine, although they have not provided a convincing explanation for the temporary interruption in intelligence sharing or the restrictions on satellite communications. Rubio said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and needed elsewhere in the world, including for the defense of the United States.
“There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” Rubio said during his visit to India.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, questioned on Tuesday whether US negotiators were acting as honest brokers in the peace process. Witkoff has met Putin repeatedly in Moscow but has visited Kyiv only once so far.
Kallas said Ukraine had resisted pressure to accept Russia's terms because of European support.
“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine had not capitulated on Putin's terms, she said, because Europe had continued to support it.
Zelensky had also told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed Washington had made a political decision to reduce assistance to Kyiv.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelensky said in Oslo, insisting that any negotiations over the country's future must include Ukrainian representatives.
He also opposed a trilateral summit proposed by Putin that would bring together the Russian president, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss a settlement for Ukraine. The Wall Street Journal reported that Zelensky would be excluded from the proposed meeting.
Trump said he was prepared to meet Putin and Xi in China next month to discuss denuclearization, adding that the talks could also address the war in Ukraine. The prospect of such a meeting has raised concerns in Kyiv that decisions about the country's future could be made without its participation.
At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. Among the victims were passengers traveling on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, where a Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of those killed was the driver of a shuttle bus traveling from the capital to a military cemetery.

articles.title: Ukraine seemed prepared for jet-powered drones, but has yet to find a solution. When will its anti-Geran weapon enter service?
articles.body:
Ukraine seemed prepared for jet-powered drones, but has yet to find a solution. When will its anti-Geran weapon enter service?
The command post of the Ukrainian Posipaky ("Minions") battalion of the 39th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment is a hive of activity. The soldiers are monitoring a large screen showing a map that is constantly updated with markers tracking drones crossing the front line. Their job is to coordinate interceptor-drone crews as they bring down Russian UAVs on the Zaporizhzhia front.
Suddenly, a new blip appears among the dozens already on the screen. It immediately catches the eye, racing along the front line at high speed. It is one of Russia's new jet-powered drones, which began appearing in large numbers in late summer.
Ramses, the battalion commander, orders his team to leave the blip alone. The drone is travelling at 500 km/h – too fast for conventional interceptor drones to bring down.
Within a few months, Russian drones crossing the front line had become a routine occurrence. The flow of UAVs continues unabated, day in, day out. But the tactics are different now: rather than launching large groups of Shaheds, Russia sends jet-powered drones one by one, at intervals of 20-30 minutes. Most get across the front line.
Long-range drones make their way into this sector from a Russian drone base in occupied Donetsk. They fly hundreds of kilometres along the front line towards the Dnipro Reservoir, where the terrain makes interception more difficult.
"They fly undetected across the occupied territories, climbing higher and gaining speed," Ramses said. "Only at the last moment do they appear on our screens, at an altitude of 5,000 to 8,000 m – well beyond the reach of MANPADS and other air defence systems."
Most of the drones are jet-powered Geran-4 loitering munitions derived from Iran's Shahed-136. But Russia is also using the newer Geran-5, which has a radically different design, more akin to a cruise missile.
These drones are piloted by an operator rather than left to fly unguided, making them even more lethal. Since losing access to Starlink, Russian forces have adopted mesh networks that use chains of drones to relay radio signals through the air. Each drone relays the signal to the preceding one, creating a link back to the operator and enabling real-time control.
"In August, Russia used around 2,400 jet-powered Gerans and 2,400 conventional ones in strikes across Ukraine," Ramses said. "Roughly a quarter to a third of those drones passed through our area of responsibility. The proportions are still roughly the same."
The Ukrainian Air Force reports that air defences managed to shoot down only 1,460 Russian jet-powered drones in August. Ukraine's ability to shoot down more jet-powered drones is hampered by a shortage of anti-aircraft missiles and a lack of high-speed interceptor drones.
Ukrainska Pravda explores why jet-powered Gerans are giving Ukraine's air defences such a hard time – and what it could take to stop them.
Russia is putting its faith in jet-powered Gerans
The arrival of jet-powered Gerans has created new opportunities for Russia to launch long-range strikes on Ukraine's rear areas. But scaling up production of the new drones is proving difficult because Russia relies on China for their jet engines.
The high failure rate of Chinese engines poses another challenge. Ukrainska Pravda has obtained a wreckage analysis by a specialist institution, which found that many drones were lost when their engines failed after several hours in the air. Repairing the engines in Russia has helped, but the problem has only been partially resolved.
As of early September, engines supplied by Chinese company Telefly began to be assembled from kits at Russia's drone production centre in Alabuga.
Russia has also begun producing the simplest structural components, suggesting plans to increase output and manufacture more components domestically.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, told Ukrainska Pravda that the new drones still contain Western electronics, including a US-made flight controller. China supplies other critical components, such as the engine, thermal imaging camera and secure communications systems.
"The Chinese side officially receives all the necessary information about the use of these components in Russian weapons," Vlasiuk said. "Yet the only response we get is that a jam-resistant satellite navigation antenna does not fall within the military goods category and is therefore not subject to the relevant export restrictions.
My latest proposal to our Chinese partners was to reclassify certain components as military goods. But I expect that they will reject it."
Trying to develop interceptor drones
Jet-powered drones are proving extremely difficult to intercept, making them one of Ukraine's most pressing air defence challenges alongside ballistic missiles. In response to this new threat, the first prototypes of high-speed interceptor drones are now reaching military units for testing.
Andrii Hrytseniuk, head of the state-run Brave1 defence technology cluster, told Ukrainska Pravda that work on a solution had begun a year before the jet-powered Geran loitering munitions started appearing en masse.
"Back in the summer of 2025, once interceptor drones had managed to close the sky to conventional Shaheds, we started looking at where to focus our efforts next," he said. "That's when we began funding teams working on solutions to take down jet-powered drones. We're talking not just about high-speed interceptors, but also anti-aircraft missiles and turrets."
Twenty-two teams have been working on high-speed drones to counter jet-powered Gerans. Twelve have received state funding from Brave1. The projects include drones equipped with miniature turbojet engines and electric-powered models with propellers.
Another promising avenue is drones powered by electric ducted fans, which resemble turbojets in design but run on battery power.
Hrytseniuk said seven interceptor drones have been deployed in combat, where they have successfully brought down jet-powered drones.
One interceptor already in service is an unidentified turbojet-powered drone spotted in use by the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU). Video footage shows it pursuing and striking a Russian Geran-5, which travels at an average speed of 500-600 km/h.
According to Hrytseniuk, the government has ordered well over 1,000 of the new interceptors. However, production is still being ramped up.
"We will definitely catch up with Russia's drone production, but it won't happen overnight," he noted. "Look at what happened with conventional Shaheds: it took us six months to scale up interceptor production. We're doing everything we can to speed things up this time, but we're not talking days or weeks."
One obstacle to scaling up production of the new interceptors is securing a supply of miniature turbojet engines. But Brave1 is confident that the issue can be resolved.
"These engines weren't available in Ukraine before," Hrytseniuk said. "No private company was making them. In 2025, we launched a programme, set up a funding scheme, made this a separate area of work and started working with manufacturers. Now, 11 Ukrainian companies are producing turbojet engines, and six of them have started mass production. It took more than a year and a half to get here."
As of early October, the new developments had not yet noticeably strengthened Ukraine's air defences. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Air Force is still doing the lion's share of the work to counter jet-powered drones, accounting for half of all successful interceptions. With missiles in short supply, pilots are using risky tactics, approaching the drones at close range to destroy them with their aircraft's cannons.
The next most effective system is the previously unknown Bars drone, which intercepted a third of the Gerans shot down in a month. It is not yet clear, however, whether this is a new interceptor or a long-range drone called Bars that has been adapted to shoot down other drones.
Drones alone are not enough
Officials and military personnel who spoke with Ukrainska Pravda warn against pinning hopes on a silver bullet that will solve all the problems. They say only a combination of different weapons, used effectively, can counter the threat posed by jet-powered Shaheds.
Another priority in tackling jet-powered drones is the development of anti-aircraft missiles that are cheaper than long-range drones and can be produced in large quantities.
Ukraine has several projects at different stages of development. Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that Luch, a Ukrainian armaments design office, had presented two missiles at the MSPO-2026 exhibition: one for the Osa air defence system and a smaller one based on the Barrier anti-tank missile system. Another company unveiled a prototype of the Shershen multi-calibre system. President Zelenskyy also mentioned the Nika small missile, which is undergoing testing.
Ukraine is also investing in missile projects led by relatively young companies. The work began within Brave1 in 2024, and developing the first prototypes took two years. Of the ten Ukrainian teams involved, two are already preparing to put their designs into operational use.
"They are cheap and easy to manufacture. One of the requirements was that each missile should cost no more than US$20,000," Hrytseniuk said.
The scale of this ambition becomes clear when compared with the market prices of existing missiles: a single Stinger can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and an AIM-9X missile fired from an F-16 costs around US$500,000.
The idea is that using two or three of these relatively cheap missiles to bring down a Russian long-range drone would still be cost-effective. Various estimates put the cost of a conventional Geran at up to US$70,000, with the jet-powered version potentially costing tens of thousands more.
Ukraine faces a tough battle to protect its strategic infrastructure in the coming months, which Russia is seeking to destroy while it has the chance. And without sufficient weapons supplies, Ukraine's military will have to rely on homegrown technology.
Only a comprehensive approach that combines the latest interceptor drones, autonomous turrets, anti-aircraft guns, aircraft, and air defence missile systems can provide effective protection.
With missiles in short supply, Ukraine has turned to domestically made automated turrets fitted with heavy machine guns. Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara said the military already has hundreds of them in service.
It will take time to work out the best mix of systems to counter the threat.
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: The Houthi war machine is evolving. Can Saudi Arabia keep pace?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The Houthi war machine is evolving. Can Saudi Arabia keep pace?
The Houthis are seeking to manufacture parts of advanced Iranian-designed medium-range ballistic missiles inside Yemen, according to new research that raises questions about how effectively Saudi Arabia can interrupt the group’s ability to sustain its attacks.
In a report published on 14 October and previewed by The Wall Street Journal, Conflict Armament Research (CAR) identified components associated with the Iranian-designed Kheibar Shekan missile family alongside industrial equipment and raw materials in shipments intended for Houthi-controlled territory.
Shipping documents identified a Chinese supplier, suggesting that the group is expanding its procurement beyond Iran-linked networks.
The findings come as Riyadh faces repeated attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure. The strikes have disrupted aviation and exposed the costs of protecting a vast country against an adversary whose arsenal and methods have developed through years of war.
For Saudi Arabia, the concern extends beyond the specifications of an individual missile. A growing ability to source components, manufacture selected parts and adapt how different weapons are used could make the Houthi strike campaign more difficult to contain.
Beyond imported missile kits
The October report concerns four containers documented by Yemeni authorities in July 2026. They had arrived in Aden’s free zone aboard two vessels in June and October 2025, carrying shipments from China whose intended destination was the Houthi-controlled port of Hodeidah.
The cargo included machined components associated with the airframe and rocket motor of the Kheibar Shekan series, one of Iran’s most advanced and longest-range ballistic missiles, together with materials and machinery potentially useful for manufacturing and testing.
Their presence points towards an effort to produce parts locally, beyond reassembling weapons delivered in separate packages.
“Inspection of the cargo revealed Houthi ambitions to at least partially manufacture medium-range ballistic missiles inside Yemen,” Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at CAR, told The New Arab. “Whether that effort has succeeded, remains a work in progress or has met major obstacles remains difficult to determine.”
Douglas Barrie, senior fellow for military aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), outlined a more limited scenario. “Final local assembly with domestic manufacturing of some components I think is most likely,” he told The New Arab.
The systems involved nevertheless represent a substantial ambition. Iran unveiled the original solid-propellant Kheibar Shekan in 2022, with a reported range of 1,450 kilometres. The missile was first used against targets in Syria in January 2024, and later against Israel and US bases in the MENA region.
CAR identifies several related variants in Houthi service, giving the group access to designs intended for long-range strikes and equipped with manoeuvring features that could complicate interception.
Earlier seizures show that the supply chain encompasses both weapons and the means to assemble or produce them. A shipment intercepted in Aden in August 2025, for example, included drone and propulsion-related equipment and advanced control components, according to US Central Command.
A separate CAR briefing, published in September, described missile kits bearing assembly labels that used Iranian rather than Houthi designations, suggesting they were produced in Iran. Broadening the supplier base would loosen that dependence.
“Sourcing components and raw materials from suppliers beyond Iran-linked networks can reduce dependence and potentially eliminate bottlenecks,” Hinz said. He cautioned that independence depends on the weapons involved: small drones built largely from commercial components are easier to manufacture than systems requiring specialised parts.
“For the more advanced weapons, the Houthis will likely continue to rely on the import of key subsystems, but further developing a domestic capability could increasingly allow for the manufacture of less sophisticated guided weapons. This would reduce dependency on external actors,” Barrie added.
Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute, sees the Chinese supply chain as a substitute for “the Iranian one, which has been severely hampered by the US naval blockade”.
The cargo documented by CAR arrived in 2025, before the current blockade, so such channels were already in use; they are likely to matter more now that Iranian routes are under pressure. Replacement has limits, however. “Houthis still depend on Iran for critical missile subsystems and guidance components,” Nadimi told The New Arab. “The Houthis cannot get those from China.”
Chinese suppliers, in other words, can provide raw materials and machined parts, but not the most sensitive components. Nor is the technology itself new. Kheibar Shekan and Fattah technology, Nadimi said, “has been transferred to Houthis for quite some time now”, though he could not say whether the group has incorporated “the latest upgrade kits”.
Iran unveiled the Fattah, which it describes as hypersonic, in 2023. The new evidence therefore concerns ambitions to manufacture parts locally, rather than the first acquisition of those technologies.
The concern predates CAR’s latest findings. On 11 September 2025, the US Treasury sanctioned Hubei Chica Industrial Co., Ltd., accusing the China-based supplier of coordinating with Houthi procurement operatives to provide chemical precursors used to manufacture ballistic missiles, explosives and other weapons inside Yemen.
The US Treasury also accused China-based Shenzhen Shengnan Trading of shipping dual-use electronics to Houthi front companies.
CAR’s evidence requires qualification. Shipping documents identified a Chinese precision-metal producer advertising custom aerospace components, but investigators have not traced the items with the manufacturer or independently verified the documentation. The findings do not establish Chinese government involvement, production volumes or a link to specific attacks on Saudi Arabia.
For Riyadh, this widens the interdiction challenge to commercial suppliers and intermediaries beyond Iran. It also gives the kingdom an incentive to seek Beijing’s cooperation on export controls and end-use checks.
An evolving strike campaign
The industrial investigation coincides with indications that the Houthis are refining how they employ their weapons. According to the Gulf Research Center, as of 15 October, the Houthis have staged at least 42 attacks on Saudi territory, including nine targeting Riyadh and five targeting energy infrastructure in the Eastern Province. At least one third of these raids involved ballistic missiles.
The Associated Press reported on 12 October that regional officials described drones preceding cruise and ballistic missiles in an attack on Riyadh airport. The sequence suggests an effort to combine weapons with different flight characteristics, although it remains unclear whether the drones acted as decoys.
“Houthis and Iranians have both tested hybrid tactics, and I am sure they compare notes too,” Nadimi told The New Arab.
Iran’s April 2024 attack on Israel combined drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, while its October 2024 attack relied exclusively on ballistic missiles. The strike on Riyadh airport followed the first pattern.
Mixed attacks require defenders to track threats across different altitudes and speeds, while repeated strikes keep personnel and equipment under pressure. Barrie cautioned that Kheibar Shekan-family missiles must be accounted for even if their actual performance falls short of advertised capabilities, “further complicating the challenges facing a defender”.
CAR’s September briefing identified another operational development: a reconnaissance drone helped cue a close-range ballistic missile against a time-sensitive target. This points to improvements in battlefield targeting, alongside the group’s expanding long-range strike capabilities.
Against Saudi Arabia, repeated attacks on airports and energy infrastructure aim to raise the costs of Riyadh’s intervention in Yemen, pressing the kingdom to scale back support for anti-Houthi forces and ease restrictions on Houthi-controlled ports and airports. The goal is bargaining power, without having to defeat Saudi forces directly.
Inside Yemen, the 15 October attack on Aden, which hit the presidential palace, exposed the internationally recognised government’s vulnerability at its own seat of power, while strikes on Marib appear intended to disrupt preparations for counteroffensives.
In the Red Sea, the threat to shipping gives the Houthis leverage over Riyadh and outside powers weighing intervention, on a trade route made more important by insecurity around the Strait of Hormuz. Their declared blockade of Saudi Arabia ties this maritime pressure to the campaign against the kingdom’s airports.
Together, these operations seek to protect Houthi territorial gains while raising the costs of attempts to reverse them. Greater military reach does not guarantee political concessions, however: attacks causing civilian casualties could instead harden Saudi resolve and draw greater external assistance.
Riyadh's containment dilemma
“They are already changing the battlefield around KSA,” Nadimi told The New Arab. For Saudi Arabia, the challenge is both immediate and cumulative: preventing the next strike while reducing the Houthis’ ability to keep launching them.
ACLED reported on 12 October that Houthi strikes and attempted strikes on Saudi territory had more than doubled over the preceding week. An airport need not be destroyed for airlines to suspend services.
Interception also consumes finite resources. Regional officials have reported pressure on Saudi interceptor stocks during the wider Iran war, making replenishment and outside assistance central to sustaining the defensive effort.
Offensive operations face a different problem: airstrikes can destroy launchers, depots and workshops, but suppressing the campaign means repeatedly locating assets that may be mobile, concealed or dispersed. Nor have Houthi air defences closed Yemeni airspace: CTP-ISW assessed on 15 October that the group’s occasional successful engagements had not significantly disrupted the Saudi air campaign.
Wider procurement networks and partial local manufacturing could make replenishment harder to interrupt, even without making the Houthis self-sufficient, while imported subsystems remain a point of vulnerability.
Riyadh’s challenge is to reduce both the group’s ability to rebuild its arsenal and the political leverage it derives from using it.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors
Follow him on X: @frencio_schiavi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: US-Iran mediation persists with both sides prep for war
articles.body:
This live blog has now closed, but our coverage of the Middle East and the region continues here.
Breadcrumb
Welcome,
Here are the updates:
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
Iranian authorities sentenced a 23-year-old student to death for blasphemy in social media posts, rights groups said, as the judiciary's use of capital punishment on political charges mounts.
Najmeh Amini was arrested in February in the northeastern city of Mashhad and sentenced to death in September on charges of insulting the Prophet Mohammed, rights groups including the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) and the Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) said in separate statements.
Iran has already hanged 34 men on charges related to the January 2026 protests. But at least eight women, as well as Amini, are facing execution on political and security charges, according to rights groups.
"I am an innocent girl. A young person with so many hopes and dreams. I have a mother and father who are waiting for me, a family who spend every night afraid of losing me until morning comes," Amini said in an audio message from prison in September that was shared by the rights groups.
"Remember my name. Perhaps I won't be able to speak anymore. But as long as I am alive, I have one hope: that before the rope becomes the end of my life, I will see a free and liberated Iran."
The use of blasphemy charges, a capital crime in the Islamic republic, had been relatively rare in recent years.
Turkey has increased its budget allocation for the procurement of weapons, ammunition, weapons systems and other defence equipment by 229% for 2027, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on Wednesday.
Presenting the government's 2027 budget proposal to parliament's planning and budget commission, Yilmaz said total allocations for defence and security would reach 3.454 trillion lira ($69.64 billion), including resources earmarked for the Defence Industry Support Fund.
The total accounts for 12.7% of the central government budget, he said.
According to the Palestinian ministry of health in Gaza, at least 74,494 people have been killed and 175,604 wounded by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023.
Since the so-called US-brokered ceasefire in October 2024, at least 1,534 Palestinians have been killed, 5,486 wounded and 846 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble, the ministry noted.
Over the past 24-hours, Israel has killed seven people and injured 24, it added.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult".
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
He added that Egypt has said it "will not enter Yemen or engage in a war against Yemen".
French President Emmanuel Macron landed in Riyadh where he is due to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Wednesday, in a surprise "solidarity" visit after weeks of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Macron is the first Western leader to visit the kingdom since Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis intensified their attacks this month.
The trip is part of a Gulf tour to secure diesel and petrol supplies as Macron seeks to bring down energy prices following violent protests in France sparked by rising living costs that have created a political crisis for the president.
"The president of the republic is travelling to Saudi Arabia this afternoon to meet with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman," a statement from Macron's office said.
The visit aimed to "demonstrate France's solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts undertaken on securing and diversifying hydrocarbon supplies", it added.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that his country would organise a conference to support the Lebanese army after Israeli elections this month, decrying what he called untenable pressure on Beirut.
Israeli troops currently occupy a swathe of south Lebanon after invading in March, while Lebanese authorities are under pressure to disarm militant group Hezbollah.
"We will coordinate to carry out this work in support of the Lebanese Armed Forces and a conference will be set up in the coming weeks by France," Macron told reporters during a visit to Qatar.
"I think it is useless to do it before the Israeli elections, but we will organise such a conference because it is unavoidable," he said.
Israel is set to go to the polls on Tuesday.
An international conference in Paris in support of Lebanon's army was planned for March but was delayed after Israel's invasion of Lebanon.
With Israel's occupation entrenched, Hezbollah rebuilding its military capabilities, and the Iran war unresolved, the threat of a new conflict looms, writes Dario Sabaghi.
Read more below:
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday targeted a military base at an airport in the southern city of Al Mukalla, which is controlled by Yemen's Saudi-backed government, two military officials told AFP.
"The Houthis used missiles and drones to target a military base housing forces from the Saudi-led coalition at Al Rayyan airport," said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia signed an agreement on Wednesday aimed at boosting defence cooperation and strengthening defensive capabilities, the Turkish Defence Ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry said the accord signed in Doha would also support military exercises and training, cooperation on research and development, and contribute to joint efforts to improve the countries' respective defence industries.
Iran is ready for diplomacy but will defend itself, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi wrote in an article published in the Financial Times on Wednesday.
"While Iran is firmly committed to seeking a dignified peaceful resolution to the conflict, we are also fully prepared to defend ourselves," he wrote.
He said the White House had shown no willingness to reach an understanding and that there was little reason to expect progress now.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that he had secured gas from Qatar during his Gulf tour, as he seeks to bring down the price of energy following violent protests sparked by rising living costs.
"We secured during the winter period the equivalent of two terawatt-hours per month of LNG, which was important for us and which will allow us to move forward," he told reporters in the Qatari capital Doha.
The US cannot expect dialogue with Iran while blockading and threatening it, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday according to state media, a day after Pakistan's army chief visited Tehran to discuss mediation efforts and regional developments.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday it had intercepted five drones launched towards the kingdom, including in the Medina region home to one of Islam's holiest cities.
"Four drones launched towards the kingdom have been intercepted and destroyed," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X, adding in a second post that the interceptions took place in Saudi Arabia's Eastern region as well as Medina.
Al-Malki, who did not specify who was behind the launches, later said another drone had been intercepted, also in the Eastern region.
The Houthis denied having targeted the kingdom, with military spokesman Yahya Saree saying their forces had not carried out any "deep" operations in Saudi territory.
Saudi Arabia has this month come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.
Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Mohammed and home to the Prophet's Mosque, is one of Islam's holiest cities alongside Mecca, both of which the Houthis have promised to spare.
Yemen's Houthis said they attacked a Saudi position in the city of Aden on Wednesday, with smoke seen rising near the airport, in the third attack in a week on the seat of power of Yemen's Riyadh-backed government.
"Our armed forces were able to target the Saudi enemy's operations room in the Badr camp in Aden with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement.
A police official in Aden earlier told AFP there had been a blast "caused by a Houthi missile", speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
Two other security sources in the city told AFP the attack targeted a site near the airport that belonged to forces from the Saudi-led military coalition that has been battling the Houthis.
An unknown projectile struck a tanker about 11 nautical miles west of Oman’s Bukha, near Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported.
UKMTO said a fire that erupted was extinguished and all crew were safe.
An explosion was heard in the Yemeni city of Aden and smoke seen rising near the airport on Wednesday, a police official and an AFP journalist said, as fighting intensifies between government forces and the Iran-backed Houthi group.
The official said the blast was "caused by a Houthi missile", speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
A missile was fired at an Iranian Kurdish opposition camp northeast of Iraq's Erbil on Wednesday, security sources said.
As Israeli settlements expand across the occupied West Bank, the West continues to peddle the myth of the two-state solution, writes Izzeddin Araj.
Read more below:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi stressed that the best solution in the region is diplomacy and reaching a negotiated solution during an interview with an Iraqi news channel.
"Our negotiations with the US side through mediating countries, including Pakistan and Qatar, are continuing continuously," he said.
"We previously presented an initiative to the US side known as the 'Seven Day Plan,' in which we clearly explained our conditions. The Strait of Hormuz was supposed to be completely opened on the sixth day of this plan. The Americans informed us that they agree to these conditions, but they would like to add some other provisions,” he added.
In response to a question about the nature of these conditions and whether they are security or economic, the Iranian minister explained that some of them are related to issues that were previously discussed during previous negotiations.
"What we want from the American side is to adhere to all the terms of the memorandum of understanding previously signed with Islamabad. After their commitment to these terms, we can enter into negotiations on other files. In the final stage of negotiations, any issue or problem raised by either party can be discussed and a final agreement can be reached," he said.
Araqchi reiterated Tehran's assertion that the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until an agreement or understanding is reached regarding it, adding: "We also said that the American side must accept our conditions for opening the Strait to ships. Before such an understanding or agreement is reached, the strait will naturally be closed, and the movement of ships in it and the current sea routes will face difficulties."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu planned to carry out strikes against Iran earlier this month, but President Donald Trump opposed reigniting the fighting before the US midterms, according to a report by the Financial Times.
Three people familiar with the matter tell the newspaper that the IDF was ready to carry out strikes on the weekend of 10 October to target Iranian nuclear facilities and regime sites, as well as civilian infrastructure including energy plants.
However, the unnamed sources say that Trump decided not to restart the conflict before the US midterms on 3 November.
The sources say the strikes would have been more intense than those carried out by the US and Israel in February.
Iraq has closed the Sheeb border crossing with Iran to passengers, vehicles and commercial trucks until further notice, two sources at the crossing said on Wednesday.
Another source said the decision has been taken to reconsider the security arrangements inside the crossing.
Israeli strikes on separate locations in the Gaza Strip killed seven Palestinians on Tuesday, according to the territory's civil defence rescue service and several hospitals.
Two men were killed in Israeli strikes in the town of Al-Zawaida and the Wadi Gaza area in the central Gaza Strip, according to Mahmoud Bassal, spokesperson of the civil defence, a rescue force operating under Hamas authority, and the Al-Aqsa Martyrs' Hospital.
An Israeli strike in the Jabalia al-Balad area in northern Gaza killed one person, according to Bassal and Al-Shifa Hospital, which reported it had received another victim of a strike in the Zeitoun neighbourhood southeast of Gaza City.
In another Israeli strike, a man and a woman, identified by Al-Shifa Hospital as Akram Yassin and his wife, were killed and several others injured in a residential block near the hospital in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, west of Gaza City.
Nasser Hospital reported that it had also received the body of a teenager killed by Israeli gunfire south of Khan Younis in Gaza's south.
ran's semi-official Nournews said on Tuesday that a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran. There was no official confirmation.
But another news agency, Tasnim, citing an unnamed source, denied such a visit.
Iran has not received a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's Houthis to its offer to help broker talks to end the fighting between them, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in a television interview aired on Tuesday.
Araqchi offered to help facilitate dialogue as the Iran-aligned Houthis intensified strikes on Saudi Arabia earlier this month.
In the interview with Iraq's Al Ekhbariya TV, Araqchi also responded to the possibility of Egypt joining Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis.
"Any foreign intervention would complicate matters," he said, adding Cairo has previously told Tehran that it would "not directly" interfere in the Yemeni conflict.
Egypt has said it is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security, potentially raising the stakes in the region.
A vote in the Egyptian parliament on a possible move against the Houthi fighters by the country's military, one of the Arab world's largest, was delayed until 26 October.

articles.title: Putin agrees to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine, US, after meeting with Witkoff
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two.
The negotiations in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia - the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher held in Russia whom US President Trump had asked the Kremlin chief to release.
Wednesday's encounter unfolded amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.
The latest talks also came more than two years after Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
The Kremlin said the new three-way peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended. They could begin sometime on or after November 10, it said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran.
The Kremlin was less upbeat, however, about the outcome of talks Witkoff had held a day earlier in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. Witkoff told Putin the talks had been characterized by "some degree of momentum" and a US official said Ukraine had brought new ideas and proposals.
"These nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the St Petersburg meeting - which lasted nearly three hours.
Possible meeting between Trump, Putin, Xi
Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, though Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing."
Putin also used Wednesday's talks to offer to help Trump deal with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear program. Putin told Witkoff it was possible and necessary to get a deal with Tehran, the Kremlin said.
Russia could also supply vast quantities of fertilizer to the United States to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff.
A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history.
New peace ideas for peace shared during meeting
Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, no NATO membership for Kyiv, and an overall peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy, was also present at the talks with Witkoff, and the Kremlin said that major joint economic projects had been discussed, including some that were close to being realized.
Witkoff said he had brought some documents with him containing various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin. Kushner later joined the meeting remotely by phone.
Zelensky said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelensky meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile.
US-Ukraine ties fray after Russian diesel export deal
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the United States. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelensky said that Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.

articles.title: Italy Investigates Russia’s Possible Role in Violent Protests
articles.body:
Italian authorities are investigating whether Russia or other foreign actors had a role in the violent cost-of-living protests that swept Milan and other European cities over the weekend, as concerns rise across the EU over Moscow’s escalating hybrid warfare.
Italy’s government, led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, has reportedly requested a briefing over what role – if any – foreign provocateurs may have played, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Oct. 21, citing people familiar with the matter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The scale of the violence and the apparent coordination of some attacks led officials to question whether the unrest was entirely spontaneous.
“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other periods,” Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said in Rome on Tuesday.
“They are the product of what I call ‘hybrid warfare,’ which someone is bringing into our countries with unconventional tools that are called TikTok, social media and YouTube, without the West realizing or reacting,” he continued, according to Bloomberg.
Meloni’s spokesperson had declined the request to comment.
Weekend unrest in Milan
According to a report from The New York Times (NYT) on Monday, Oct. 19, thousands of people were brought to the streets by rising food and fuel prices, combined with low wages, high taxes and public spending cuts.
Ukraine Counts on Beijing’s ‘Constructive Role’ as Sybiha Meets Chinese Ambassador
Milan reportedly saw the largest turnout, with about 2,000 demonstrators according to the city’s police, while protests also took place in Bologna, Turin, Brescia and Bergamo.
The initial call to protest came from an anonymous social media account created earlier in October, which urged nationwide anti-government demonstrations to “bring the birth of a new Italy and a new Europe.”
While most participants in Milan marched peacefully, masked groups looted shops, set fires and threw objects at police, who responded with water cannons and tear gas.
War just meters from the Milan cathedral, Duomo. The symbol of Christianity in Italy and Europe, surrounded by smoke bombs, firecrackers and police vans under attack. This is not a protest. This is urban guerrilla warfare in the heart of our history and faith. And many of those… pic.twitter.com/vqD4612ReR
— RadioGenoa (@RadioGenoa) October 18, 2026
The NYT reported that police arrested 32 people, most of them minors, and reported 14 officers injured. A local business association put the damage at more than €1 million (roughly $1.1 million).
“Demonstrating is a right, devastating our cities is not,” Meloni said in a statement on X.
The unrest mirrored similar movements elsewhere in Europe, including student-led riots in France, the country’s worst in decades.
In southern Italy, farmers and truckers have blockaded ports and highways over soaring fuel prices linked to the war in Iran.
Troops deployed to Milan
Crosetto also said that children as young as 11 or 12 who took part appeared to have undergone a form of “counter-education.” He, however, offered no further details on what that would entail.
With more demonstrations expected this weekend, the government announced the deployment of 500 military personnel in Milan until the end of the year.
According to Bloomberg, opposition critics accused Meloni’s conservative coalition of exploiting the unrest ahead of the next year’s elections while neglecting grievances behind it.
Meloni’s firm line on Moscow
