articles.title: Putin agrees to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and US
articles.body:
Putin agrees to resume talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin says
In short:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
The Russian leader has met with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
What's next?
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he supports the proposal, and is hopeful the three-way talks will take place in early November.
The Kremlin says Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
The Russian leader met US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg.
Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said the focus would be on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends".
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Mr Witkoff's talks with Mr Putin about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as US President Donald Trump pushed Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that only a leaders' summit can break the impasse.
Latest proposals have little of value, Kremlin says
The Kremlin said the discussion in St Petersburg lasted about three hours and came a day after Mr Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
Mr Ushakov said the proposals from the Oslo meeting "contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis".
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow was not "fully satisfied" with the Oslo proposals, they were a step in the right direction.
Mr Zelenskyy said he supported the proposal for three-way talks.
"We have received feedback that … Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams," he said.
"The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that …The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November."
Mr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives".
Witkoff sees 'some degree of momentum' in peace efforts
Mr Witkoff and Mr Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Mr Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table.
Mr Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link.
Before the meeting, Mr Witkoff said that there was "some degree of momentum" in talks.
In televised opening remarks, Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin for agreeing to send diesel to the US after Mr Trump lifted a ban despite anger from some US lawmakers, adding that the fuel would help reduce prices for American farmers and truckers.
Mr Putin said he was ready to consider restoring US-Russia economic ties and was prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran.
He said Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace.
Mr Ushakov said that "large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation" between Russia and the US were discussed in detail with Mr Witkoff.
"Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage," he said.
Russia resumes attacks on Ukraine
Just as Russia indicated its readiness to join the trilateral peace talks, officials in Ukraine reported the capital Kyiv had been attacked with ballistic missiles on Wednesday evening, local time.
Homes, a petrol station and transport equipment were damaged and six people were injured.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram there were strikes in two districts on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, and posted on social media:
"Explosions in the capital. Kyiv is under ballistic attack.
"Stay in shelters!"
The city remained under a drone warning for more than two hours after the initial alert was declared.
AP/Reuters

articles.title: Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
articles.body:
Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
Tehran had ‘nothing new’ to tell Washington after latest nuclear proposals reportedly offered by mediators.
Tehran, Iran – There has been a flurry of diplomatic activity in the Middle East in recent days, with hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to end the United States and Israel war on Iran.
Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir was in Tehran on Wednesday to discuss the war and recent tensions in Yemen. It comes against the backdrop of fears of a new breakout in conflict in the region.
Despite this, Tehran has held firm to its position that the war will not end, and the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen, until the US accepts its conditions.
Iran maintains an unyielding stance on its contentious nuclear programme, which was a factor in the Trump administration’s decision to launch the war on February 28.
“Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said late Tuesday after meeting Munir.
But he did not rule out downblending the highly enriched uranium inside the country under supervision from monitors, something Iran has offered before.
Iran’s authorities present the decades-old nuclear programme as a sovereign right and an achievement gained despite strikes, sabotage and assassinations. Rezaei described it as “national wealth” on Tuesday.
Iran has also used low-enriched uranium for civilian purposes like manufacturing radiopharmaceuticals and for power generation at the Bushehr plant in cooperation with Russia.
The authorities argue that surrendering the nuclear programme under military pressure would amount to capitulation, if it did not guarantee that Iran would not be left exposed to more attacks.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly emphasised since the start of the war that he wanted to dismantle the Iranian nuclear programme. US Vice President JD Vance, however, suggested earlier this month that a “meaningful” reduction in the level of enrichment capacity may satisfy US demands.
Nuclear issue
Before Israeli and US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Tehran possessed 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. A nuclear bomb would need enrichment of more than 90 percent.
The attacks, followed by further US-Israeli strikes on nuclear sites in 2026, severely damaged Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. With the IAEA unable to inspect key facilities, the current size, condition and whereabouts of much of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile remain unverified.
Tehran has refused access to the IAEA to inspect its nuclear facilities since the war started, accusing the agency of advancing Western interests through adopting resolutions and referring the nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council.
Iranian authorities maintain they are not pursuing a bomb. But senior Iranian officials, like Rezaei, have publicly questioned the validity of being a party to the international nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty if Iran’s nuclear facilities and other infrastructure continue to be attacked.
Still, Iranian officials have hosted numerous foreign diplomats this week. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was in Tehran on Monday after attending a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries a day earlier. There were also indications of visits to Tehran by other Arab officials.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also reported to have met Israeli security officials earlier this week. These meetings did not appear to have decreased the prospects of renewed war.
But speaking at a conference for Iranian exporters in Tehran on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi cautioned that the country faces threats of more attacks and expansive economic sanctions.
“The reality is that the country is truly in war conditions and the war continues. We have not reached peace conditions and are away from it, so all decisions must be made within war conditions,” he said.
Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Munir that Iran had “nothing new” to tell Washington and expected realisation of conditions offered in New York last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
Mediators did not publicly divulge details of their proposals to Tehran this week, but were told the US needed to build trust by accepting Iran’s conditions. These include returning to the June memorandum of understanding and recognising an Iran-Oman deal over temporary transit in the Strait of Hormuz.
In addition to a pledge for immediate talks on a bigger deal regarding Iran’s nuclear issue, the memorandum included removing the US naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, waivers for oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and halting military action in Lebanon and other regional hotspots.
Ellie Geranmayeh, a senior policy fellow and deputy head of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said it was clear that Tehran would be unwilling to give up its enriched uranium without guarantees of sanctions relief.
“The Iranians have made it very clear, and I see no evidence that’s changing, that they are willing to negotiate over the fate of the highly enriched uranium or access for international monitors, but that has to be directly linked with a very clear implementation protocol for US sanctions relief,” she told Al Jazeera. “We are very far from those types of negotiations at this stage.”
US media cited unnamed officials as saying on Tuesday that the Pentagon was sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and a Marine unit to the Middle East. That would present President Trump with a range of strike options after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Over recent weeks, Trump and his officials have further discussed a range of military operations, including hitting Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain to diminish nuclear facilities inside, and dropping the “mother of all bombs” on nuclear and energy facilities. They have also previously raised the idea of seizing Iran’s southern islands on the Strait of Hormuz and assassinating more Iranian officials.
Iran’s state-run Press TV cited an unnamed security official as saying on Wednesday that decision-makers in Tehran have chosen to advance “without any limitations or restraint” if there are more US and Israeli attacks or assassinations.
Geranmayeh pointed out that Tehran had also helped its ally, the Houthis in Yemen, with their advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and even considered potential preemptive strikes to rattle the US ahead of the election.
“One thing we should be watching out for is Israel and the US combining forces on military attacks after the Israeli elections and the US midterms,” she said, after Trump backed Netanyahu’s election bid.

articles.title: Trump’s Rift With Zelensky Raises European Fears
articles.body:
European officials and diplomats increasingly believe that US President Donald Trump’s hostility toward Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and apparent preference for Russian President Vladimir Putin are shaping Washington’s approach to the war, according to comments by European officials and former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, POLITICO reports.
Trump signaled this week that he did not consider Russia equally responsible for the war, saying, “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine. They have not been doing that much.”
The remarks reinforced concerns in Kyiv, which has endured weeks of intensifying Russian bombardment, and among Ukraine’s European allies that Washington is siding with Moscow.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday that US negotiators had spent nearly two years trying to force Ukraine to surrender. She said continued European assistance had prevented Kyiv from accepting Russia’s demands.
Some European officials and diplomats attribute Trump’s latest shift against Ukraine partly to his personal preferences rather than solely to US political objectives.
“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said Lidington, now a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. He argued that Trump’s self-centered approach, affinity for dictators and autocrats, and desire to create opportunities for US businesses were significant factors in his decision-making.
EU officials share that assessment privately. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky. He just doesn’t like him,” a government official who has closely observed both leaders said. The official added that this personal animosity complicated efforts to secure US assistance for peace, noting that Trump generally treated matters as business transactions, but not consistently.
An EU diplomat, speaking anonymously to discuss sensitive issues, said Trump’s unpredictable behavior meant he could reverse his recent actions against Ukraine. However, the diplomat identified one consistent feature of his approach: “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”
The diplomat said Trump had criticized Ukraine, the European Union and NATO but had rarely directed criticism at Putin. “We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ukraine and its European partners face mounting difficulties if Trump's attitude toward Zelensky proves impossible to change. After four-and-a-half years of war, Kyiv is running short of funding and air defenses, while growing support for Europe's populist right could undermine political backing for Ukraine in the coming months.
Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff, met Zelensky and the leaders of Norway and Finland for talks in Oslo on Tuesday. He is due to travel to St. Petersburg on Wednesday for discussions with Russian leaders on peace proposals as the White House intensifies its push for a ceasefire. One proposal under consideration is a three-way summit involving Trump, Zelensky and Putin.
Previous attempts to bring Putin to such a meeting have failed, and EU diplomats see no genuine indication that the Russian leader wants a ceasefire. They consider Trump's antagonism toward Zelensky particularly damaging in that context.
“There is a clear consensus across Europe that Putin does not want peace,” a second EU diplomat said. “He will need to be forced into peace.”
Rather than increasing pressure on Putin, Trump has intensified his demands on Zelensky, even as Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities have escalated this month. According to the first EU diplomat, Zelensky described the strain he was under during private meetings with European Union counterparts in Brussels last week.
Trump has made a series of sharply critical statements about the Ukrainian leader in recent days, accusing him of not caring and refusing to end the war, while suggesting that he should be replaced either as president or as Ukraine's negotiator.
“President Putin would like to see a settlement,” Trump said. “President Zelensky could have solved this war, or he could have made a deal, many times.”
Lidington suggested that Trump's animosity toward Zelensky might have originated in 2019, during Trump's first term, when he pressed the Ukrainian leader to assist with an investigation into Joe Biden, who later defeated Trump in the presidential election. Subsequent confrontations, including a hostile meeting in the Oval Office in February 2025, further strengthened that impression, he said.
“It was clear that in the infamous meeting in the White House that Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance had planned that public beating-up of Zelensky and it struck me then that there was a strong personal element to this,” Lidington said.
He also pointed to Trump's preference for authoritarian leaders, arguing that the president tends to seek closer relations with strongmen who fit a particular image.
Lidington recalled a dinner in Paris in 2018 marking the centenary of the end of World War I, hosted jointly by French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Angela Merkel at the time. Trump showed little interest in making small talk with either leader, he said.
“It was pretty obvious from the body language that Trump was impatient with them and one of the people he really wanted to talk to was [Turkish leader Recep Tayyip] Erdoğan and other people who were a bit more in that strongman image that he likes to portray himself,” Lidington said.
A senior European official familiar with the Ukraine negotiations offered a broader explanation, saying Trump's motivations involved political calculations, potential profits and personal relationships.
“They are currently in an election cycle and need someone to blame for rising prices,” the official said. The official added that Trump was drawn to different kinds of personalities and leaders, particularly successful and cheerful people.
Zelensky has warned in recent days that the reduction in US assistance has contributed to higher civilian casualties in Ukraine. He cited cuts affecting Starlink and Starshield services, which Ukraine uses to defend itself against Russian attacks and plan operations.
“We still have no explanation for this, just different strange stories,” Zelensky told US congressmen on Monday.
Ukraine has also faced problems receiving advance warnings of incoming Russian missile attacks from US partners, which have not been delivered as usual this month, Zelensky said. He added that the country was running low on Patriot missile interceptors.
The Pentagon has not issued an official response to Ukraine's complaints.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported that 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 injured across the country last month, an increase of 85% compared with September 2025. The UN also said the first two weeks of October ranked among the deadliest periods for Ukrainian civilians in years, as missile and drone attacks intensified.
The first EU diplomat cited above said many European governments were frustrated that Trump had excluded them from his discussions with Putin so far.
“There is probably much more dialogue between the Americans and the Russians than we might know,” the diplomat said.
Witkoff's meeting with Zelensky in Norway on Tuesday raised the possibility that direct engagement with Putin could again become an option for the Ukrainian president.
After participating in the Oslo talks, Finnish President Alexander Stubb expressed optimism about the negotiations.
“Today was a good day for peace,” Stubb said. He added that substantial and technical progress had been made quietly over the preceding week and that he believed the process had returned to the right track.
Stubb said the negotiations were moving in the right direction again, adding, “Hopefully, we don’t do any backtracking.”

articles.title: WSJ: Elon Musk personally ordered Starlink restrictions for Ukraine
articles.body:
WSJ: Elon Musk personally ordered Starlink restrictions for Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal has written that Elon Musk ordered the speed of the military version of Starlink to be reduced in Ukraine, leaving some Ukrainian attack and interceptor drones practically unusable.
Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing sources
Details: The WSJ noted that both Musk and US President Donald Trump have expressed dissatisfaction with Ukraine over its strikes on Russian oil refineries in recent weeks. Trump sees these attacks as a reason for high energy prices.
Sources told the WSJ that Musk was behind the restriction of the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the satellite network last week, rendering some attack and interceptor drones practically useless.
Two sources said Musk and Trump had discussed the decision on Starlink during a phone call shortly after news of the speed restrictions became public.
One source also claimed that Musk and Trump had discussed the issue even before the decision to restrict Starlink speeds was made.
Public complaints by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said Ukrainians could die if unrestricted access to the service was not restored, led to widespread confusion over who had ordered the speed reduction and an unofficial investigation at the White House.
According to the sources, as the controversy unfolded, SpaceX representatives contacted their counterparts at the White House in an attempt to reach a common understanding and issue a joint statement saying that the company and Trump's administration had coordinated their actions before Musk issued the order.
Hours after news of the speed reduction became public, Musk wrote on X (Twitter): "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," using the acronym for president of the United States.
Trump told journalists on 19 October that he did not know who was responsible for reducing Starlink speeds, "but I would like to find out".
Some US officials claim that Musk had acted unilaterally and that Trump had not specifically ordered any retaliatory measures against Ukraine.
However, a source familiar with the situation said Musk had spoken to several administration officials, including Trump, before introducing the new speed restriction. Ukrainian officials said the restriction had allowed Russian missiles to bypass their air defence systems.
Background:
- Reuters reported earlier that the order to restrict Starshield, a satellite system Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and to control interceptor drones, came directly from the White House.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

articles.title: Witkoff arrives in Russia for Putin talks on Ukraine
articles.body:
The United States special envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in the Russian city of Saint Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the war in Ukraine.
The state-run Russian news agency Tass reported the arrival. Witkoff is scheduled to meet Putin during the “first half” of the day at the Constantine Palace, according to Yuri Ushakov, an adviser to Putin.
“Yes, he is going to meet with Putin in the Constantine Palace,” Ushakov said.
The palace was constructed in the 1700s and is used today for official events.
“Negotiations on the Ukraine conflict are of course the main topic of today’s meeting,” Ushakov said, according to Tass.
Before traveling to Russia, Witkoff was in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Representatives from France, Britain, Germany, Poland, the European Union, and NATO also attended the meeting in Oslo.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the Tuesday meeting “positive.”
“Equipped with those ideas, he can now go to Saint Petersburg and share them with Russia – and let us see if we can make some progress,” Rubio said, according to the news agency AFP.
U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner is also expected to take part in the meeting with Putin by video link, an American official told AFP.
Witkoff is scheduled to land in Oslo again on his way back from Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told the Norwegian media outlet NRK.
“It will probably be a meeting at the airport, I think. The expectation is presumably that it will be some form of feedback. I think perhaps that we are in a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre said.
Relations between Ukraine and the United States have experienced tension recently after U.S. President Donald Trump made a diesel deal with Russia and voiced criticism of Zelenskyy.
After the Oslo talks, Zelenskyy said that the warnings about ballistic missiles that Ukraine gets from the United States are “working” again.
“It is very important for the people, because then we know when the Russian ballistic missiles are coming,” Zelenskyy wrote on the social media platform X.

articles.title: Russia Surrounds Major Shahed Drone Production Hub With 33 Air Defense Positions in Tatarstan
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia Surrounds Major Shahed Drone Production Hub With 33 Air Defense Positions in Tatarstan
Russia has built 33 air defense positions around the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, a major production hub for Shahed-type attack drones, according to satellite imagery from October 21 analyzed by Radio Liberty.
The images show a substantial expansion of air defense infrastructure around one of Russia's primary facilities for manufacturing Geran-type drones, derived from Iranian Shahed designs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Since spring 2026, Russian forces have constructed several concrete towers for air defense systems and additional elevated platforms designed to accommodate Pantsir or Tor short-range air defense systems.
The Pantsir combines surface-to-air missiles and automatic cannons to intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, and drones. The Tor is a mobile short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to engage aerial targets, including precision-guided weapons and unmanned aircraft.
The report also identified towers equipped with heavy anti-aircraft machine guns inside the Alabuga complex. Additional structures have been installed to support anti-drone nets stretched over production buildings, providing another protective layer against aerial attacks.
The extensive fortifications make Alabuga one of Russia's most heavily protected facilities against Ukrainian drone strikes. Radio Liberty noted that Ukrainian drones last reached the site in June 2025, with no comparable attacks recorded there since.
The scale of the protective buildup reflects Alabuga’s growing weight in Russia's drone program. The complex has reportedly reached a capacity of more than 3,000 gasoline-powered Shahed-type drones and more than 3,500 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month.
Chinese suppliers have been linked to that expansion, providing an industrial airframe production line, more than 685,000 engine components valued at about $900,000, and 7,800 lithium-ion batteries in 2024. Chinese technology also contributed to navigation systems designed to withstand electronic warfare, including satellite antennas that were reportedly exported as agricultural products.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Pentagon chief denies directives restricting Starshield in Ukraine, points to priority of replenishing US air defense arsenals
articles.body:
The US Department of War maintains an unchanged position on supporting Ukraine and has refrained from issuing any directives on restricting the operation of the Starshield satellite network, while on the supply of interceptor missiles Washington's priority is to provide its own armed forces with as many as possible, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said.
"We have not changed our position on the Ukrainians in any way, but on things like interceptor missiles, of course, we want to make sure our guys are also supplied with as many as possible. So that is the case, and President Zelenskyy knows it," Hegseth said.
According to Hegseth, press reports about a change in the Pentagon's approach to Ukraine are false. He noted the heroic efforts of Ukrainians and recalled that under the previous American administration Kyiv was given large volumes of military aid that drained American stockpiles, so the department is now replenishing these stocks on the instruction of US President Donald Trump.
Commenting on reports about reduced speeds and restricted coverage of the Starshield military satellite system in Ukraine, the Pentagon chief assured that the US defense department had left service volumes unreduced and had refrained from issuing such orders. Hegseth explained that the use of terminals is governed by the terms of service, and the authority to decide on compliance with them rests directly with the Starlink operator, and he wished the Ukrainian side success.
As reported, the administration of US President Donald Trump is holding back, without consideration, the transfer of anti-aircraft interceptor missiles for Patriot systems for Ukraine from partner countries, which coincides with a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations between Washington and Kyiv over disagreements about strikes on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: Dozens of Israeli fighter jets flew to Iran's border in exercise that risked 'miscalculation': report
articles.body:
Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets conducted an operational flight on Monday, approaching the Iranian border, Axios reported, citing Israeli and American officials. The mission, which took place approximately 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from Israel, came a week before the elections and on the same day that U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Ovda Air Force Base. According to the report, the flight was unrelated to Hegseth's visit.
Meanwhile, following Netanyahu's statement that Tehran is "once again trying to develop its bombs of death," and a report that U.S. President Donald Trump had blocked an Israeli strike on Iran, American officials told Reuters that the State Department intends to evacuate some diplomatic personnel and their families from Saudi Arabia. According to the officials, the move stems from concerns about renewed fighting, particularly involving the Houthis in Yemen.
Israeli and American officials told Axios that the flight, involving dozens of fighter jets and aerial refueling aircraft, was not unusual and was intended to deter the Islamic Republic. However, they noted that it could have led to a "miscalculation," triggering an Iranian response and reigniting the war. The flight path followed a potential route for an attack on Iran, passing through Syrian and Iraqi airspace. As the aircraft approached the Iranian border, they changed course and returned to Israel.
American officials said the Israelis knew that Iran's air defense systems would detect the aircraft. According to the sources, Israel notified the United States in advance and described the operation as an exercise intended to demonstrate strength and deter Iran from attacking Israel ahead of the elections. However, several American sources said they were under the impression that Israel had hoped Iranian forces would fire at the aircraft, providing justification for launching strikes against Iran.
Earlier this month, Netanyahu told Trump he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating that Iran was taking alarming steps to rebuild its nuclear program. At a military officers' graduation ceremony on Wednesday, he made that warning explicit.
"Mojtaba has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again trying to develop its bombs of death," Netanyahu said. "Therefore, there is only one way to eliminate this threat once and for all: to overthrow the regime in Iran. And that is the directive I have given the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies."
Following Netanyahu's warning, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir told Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, that renewing the war at this time could lead to the postponement of the elections, as Iran would likely retaliate.
Trump initially appeared inclined to resume the strikes, but later hesitated and ultimately decided not to accept Netanyahu's proposal. An Israeli official said Zamir would not allow unjustified military action that could jeopardize next week's elections.

articles.title: Britain’s cargo drone becomes a low-cost drone interceptor
articles.body:
- A BAE Systems TRV-150 drone armed with a three-pod APKWS launcher intercepted several attack drones during a Pentagon experiment at Eglin Air Force Base.
- The adapted Malloy T-150 fired laser-guided rockets at multiple targets in one flight without landing to reload.
A heavy-lift cargo drone built by BAE Systems subsidiary Malloy Aeronautics has shot down several one-way attack drones with laser-guided rockets during a Pentagon experiment in Florida, firing one rocket after another without having to land and reload.
The modified aircraft, known as the TRV-150, carried a three-pod launcher loaded with BAE Systems’ APKWS rockets during the Joint Readiness Experimentation exercise run by the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering at Eglin Air Force Base from Sept. 21 to 25, BAE Systems said in a statement on Oct. 21.
The TRV-150 is a version of Malloy’s T-150 quadcopter, a British-built electric drone designed to carry cargo, which Maryland-based SURVICE Engineering adapted to meet U.S. Army requirements while BAE Systems’ FalconWorks division developed the APKWS kit and integrated it on the aircraft. BAE Systems says the trials show that low-cost precision weapons can be fitted to uncrewed platforms to counter drone threats on the battlefield, and the company now wants to take the same setup to sea to protect ships from similar attacks.
“Our customers are facing drone threats right now, so we’ve worked at pace with our partners to move from concept to a proven system, which can engage multiple targets in a single mission,” said Thomas Lancashire, head of UAS business development at BAE Systems FalconWorks.
APKWS, short for Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, turns an ordinary unguided 70 mm (2.75-inch) Hydra rocket into a precision weapon by fitting a laser-guidance section between the warhead and the motor, which makes it far cheaper than the air-to-air missiles traditionally used to shoot down drones. The rocket has become one of the U.S. military’s main low-cost answers to cheap attack drones, and in May the U.S. Navy awarded L3Harris a contract worth up to $98.4 million for proximity fuzes that make APKWS more effective against drones, while BAE Systems test-fired the rocket from a Royal Air Force Typhoon in March as it adds counter-drone rockets to the fighter.
The Eglin trials build on the first firing of a precision munition from an adapted T-150 in July 2025, when the drone launched a single APKWS rocket, and this time the team used a production-ready three-pod launcher to engage targets in the air. The ability to fire several shots in one sortie matters against attack drones, which often arrive in groups and leave little time for a launcher to land, reload and take off again.
“Supporting the warfighter has been at the core of SURVICE’s mission since its founding over 45 years ago. Bringing the TRV-150 to the US warfighter and now adding APKWS as a proven, precise, and cost-effective capability to our TRV-150 UAS platform is exactly the type of innovation SURVICE was designed to deliver,” said Gregory Thompson, president of SURVICE Engineering.
BAE Systems bought Malloy Aeronautics in 2024, and the T-150 is already in service with British forces as a logistics drone. During the Royal Navy Carrier Strike Group’s eight-month deployment to the Indo-Pacific last year, the drone carried supplies between ships throughout the voyage, and SURVICE is one of several partners BAE Systems is working with around the world to turn the aircraft into a multi-role counter-drone system.
BAE Systems has not said when an armed TRV-150 could enter service, but the company’s next step is to adapt the rocket-armed version for maritime use, where it would help defend ships against the kind of drone attacks that have hit vessels in the Red Sea and the Black Sea.

articles.title: Rostec develops attack drones with characteristics comparable to cruise missiles
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Russia’s state corporation Rostec is developing and manufacturing strike drones with performance characteristics on par with those of cruise missiles, the corporation said.
"As technology advances, the distinction between a drone, a cruise missile, and a loitering munition is disappearing. The Dan-T is already a full-fledged cruise missile in terms of its capabilities. The Rostec State Corporation is working to advance this field, and several other comparable projects are underway. These systems are becoming increasingly intelligent – all of them feature elements of artificial intelligence to one degree or another.
The next models, which we will be able to present as early as next year, will fly farther, faster, and will be considerably more advanced in terms of intelligence," Rostec said in a video presentation of its latest Dan-T aerial strike drone.
The state corporation presented this system at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 in Egypt.
About the munition
The Dan-T is a loitering munition with a range of up to 450 km. With a weight of up to 270 kilograms and equipped with a compact turbojet engine, it can be launched from both aircraft and helicopters. The Dan-T is designed to fly in stealth mode to evade air defense systems and operates fully autonomously after launch from its carrier. The munition can approach its target at speeds of up to 500 km/h while following the terrain, thereby reducing the likelihood of interception by enemy air defense systems.
The Dan-T can be launched from Russian-designed aircraft and helicopters, including the Yak-130, MiG-29, Mi-28N, and Mi-8. It can also be integrated with foreign combat aircraft.
As Rostec told TASS, the munition’s effectiveness has been confirmed by hundreds of successful launches against enemy targets during the special military operation in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine’s top war charity names only way to save $25,000 to $4 million each time cheap Russian jet-powered drone is shot down
articles.body:
Intercepting a jet-powered Geran can cost anywhere from $2,000 to $4 million depending on the weapon used. Cheap interceptor drones are the only option that keeps air defense affordable, the foundation of Ukrainian top war volunteer Serhii Sternenko said on Telegram.
Russia’s jet Gerans now carry every characteristic of a small cruise missile, and Russians keep raising their speed in answer to each Ukrainian countermeasure. Former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi has framed the shift bluntly: an expensive Cold War missile has become a cheap weapon fired in bulk, and the drone is now “a missile in all but name,” affordable to any side, not only wealthy countries.
Sternenko heads a charitable foundation that has purchased 291,502 FPV drones, which have helped Ukraine’s military down more than 12,954 aerial targets. Also, has advised the team of former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Three ways to kill a jet Geran, and what each costs
The foundation laid out the price of each method:
- Aircraft (F-16, MiG-29, Su-27, Mirage 2000): $25,000 to $1.2 million per kill. Effective, but the stock of missiles is critically low, and some air-to-air types are no longer being replenished.
- Surface-to-air and shoulder-fired systems (IRIS-T, NASAMS, Vampire, Avenger): about $30,000 to $4 million. Good for shielding key sites, but a missile capable of reaching a jet Geran at 6 to 7 kilometers costs $0.5 million to $4 million.
- Interceptor drones (makers undisclosed): from $2,000. Cheap, with trained operators ready, but not yet scalable.
Why the cheapest option is the one that matters
No single tool is enough, the foundation stresses. Downing jet Gerans still needs aircraft, small aviation and missile systems together, but it is the interceptors that make the defense affordable, taking out the cheaper Shaheds and saving costly missiles for targets nothing else can reach.
The foundation says it has found a way to counter drones that already match small cruise missiles, working with Ukrainian manufacturers, without disclosing details. The method is far cheaper than other ways of downing jet Gerans and significantly strengthens air defense, it says, as part of a wider Ukrainian push to field interceptor drones fast enough to catch Russia’s fastest weapons.
Read also
- War-hit Kyiv puts 85 European-funded buses on its streets. Here’s what riders find inside
- Ukraine’s Navy killed Russian Shahed: one drone boat launched another drone, which shot down third, all unmanned, all at sea
- Ukraine sends ground robot to string wire obstacles in open, taking its sappers out of kill zone

articles.title: Putin and U.S. envoy Witkoff hold talks in St. Petersburg as Washington pushes a new plan to end the war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Putin and U.S. envoy Witkoff hold talks in St. Petersburg as Washington pushes a new plan to end the war in Ukraine
Steve Witkoff, the U.S. president’s special envoy, flew to St. Petersburg this morning for a meeting with Vladimir Putin, part of a renewed U.S. effort to restart talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. Jared Kushner, the U.S. president’s son-in-law, who usually accompanies Witkoff on such trips, did not travel to Russia because of illness but is taking part in the meeting by video link.
Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian president’s special representative, met Witkoff at Pulkovo Airport. The meeting with Putin began around noon Moscow time at Konstantinovsky Palace, and its opening was open to the press. Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing to the “diesel deal” and said he hoped the Russian president would consider resuming trilateral talks. He also said he had brought documents outlining approaches to a peaceful settlement.
Putin announced that Russia had released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had fought for Ukraine’s armed forces. After he fell into Russian captivity, a court sentenced him to nearly seven years in prison on charges of mercenary activity.
Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo the day before his meeting with Putin. The talks also included Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and representatives from the EU, NATO, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Poland. Kushner took part in the meeting online.
After the talks, Stubb said they had made “real progress on two levels”: in the short term and in a broader context. He said the discussions touched on key issues including air defense, energy facilities, and the possibility of a partial ceasefire.
Zelensky said Ukraine and the West have “clear ideas about how to achieve peace,” including organizing a trilateral meeting with Trump, Putin, and Zelensky himself “to resolve issues that only leaders can resolve.”
Moscow has repeatedly said it sees the point of that meeting only in the final stages of negotiations. After the talks in Oslo, Trump said he believes Putin and Zelensky do not “don’t have to be in the same room” at a trilateral meeting.
Sources cited by Axios said the discussions in Oslo focused on drafting a framework agreement to end the war, which would then be proposed to Russia. The outlet reported that the parties made “meaningful progress” and reached a “strong alignment at the working level” on further steps. Axios sources said Kushner again asked Ukraine at the meeting to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Witkoff is expected to leave Moscow later today and return to Oslo, where he will meet again with Norwegian Prime Minister Støre to brief him on his talks with Putin.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Stubb calls for Ukraine-Russia-US peace talks as Trump envoy meets Putin
articles.body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has called for direct negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the United States over disputed territories and security guarantees, as US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, to discuss proposals for ending the war.
Stubb outlined Europe's priorities during a speech at the University of Helsinki, a day after participating in eight hours of discussions in Oslo involving Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Witkoff and representatives from NATO and the European Union.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
According to Stubb, the Oslo meeting sought to ease tensions between Washington and Kyiv, establish European and Ukrainian priorities ahead of Witkoff's meeting with Putin, and agree on the next steps towards negotiations.
The Finnish president said the central objective was to arrange bilateral or trilateral talks addressing territorial disputes, which remain among the main obstacles to an agreement.
He identified US security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe's security arrangements after the war as further priorities. Negotiators would also need to address ceasefire monitoring, the location of military contact lines, energy security, food supplies and prisoner exchanges.
Stubb said the eventual agreement would involve compromises concerning territory and security guarantees, including the question of whether Ukraine receives bilateral US commitments or NATO membership.
Speaking about the Oslo discussions, Stubb said negotiations behind closed doors differed considerably from the public exchanges between Washington and Kyiv.
Witkoff subsequently travelled to St Petersburg for his ninth meeting with Putin, carrying documents outlining proposals for a possible peace settlement.
"One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about the resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia and the United States," Witkoff told Putin, according to Reuters.
A US official told Reuters that the Oslo discussions had produced "meaningful progress" towards a coordinated approach to Russia, including proposals covering Ukrainian security guarantees, economic reconstruction and European security.
The meeting in Russia also coincided with the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher imprisoned in Russia on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
According to The Guardian, Putin ordered Hubbard's release following a personal request from Trump. The release did not involve a prisoner exchange.
Trump confirmed on Truth Social that Russia had released Hubbard without requiring concessions from Washington.
Witkoff praised Putin during their meeting, describing him as a humanitarian and thanking him for the gesture.
The discussions took place amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv following Trump's agreement to resume Russian diesel imports and Ukrainian complaints about restrictions on US intelligence sharing and military satellite communications.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday's Oslo meeting had helped resolve some intelligence-sharing problems.
Russia continues to demand control over the entire Donetsk region and opposes Ukrainian NATO membership, while Kyiv seeks security guarantees and an end to Russian attacks.
Putin also raised prospects for economic cooperation with Washington, including fertiliser exports, and offered Russian assistance concerning Iran.
In Helsinki, Stubb addressed the wider implications of changes in US foreign policy, warning that relations between Europe and Washington had undergone a lasting transformation.
"There is no return to the old transatlantic relationship," Stubb said.
HT

articles.title: Kyiv’s Donors Expected Peace in 2027, but Russian Escalations Left 2026 Funding Unfulfilled
articles.body:
Each year since Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s donors have bet on peace the following year.
Each year, Moscow has proved them wrong.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
As of late 2026, Ukraine has been trying to work out how to counter jet-powered Russian drones, which have caused more civilian deaths and cost $1.5 billion in tax revenues by year-end, per the prime minister’s estimates. Moscow is also expanding the Alabuga-Volokno factory to raise Geran/Shahed drone production by 78%, according to Politico, even as the IMF reported that its economy grew only 1% this year.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko told Ukrinform that Russia may have enough resources to continue until 2028. And the Bank of Finland Institute for Emerging Economies (BOFIT) wrote in its mid-term forecast that Russia can still sustain a full-scale war thanks to higher oil prices, despite weaker economic activity and a widening fiscal deficit.
“Even with the risks of continuing the war, there are no signs that the economy faces an immediate collapse into crisis,” it wrote in its latest Forecast for Russia for 2026-28.
Kyiv’s mission: two months to find almost $50 billion
The aid plans assume a happier ending in 2027, which isn’t the case in Ukraine.
In autumn 2026, the finance ministry received a bill from the defense ministry for an additional $27 billion to fund costlier warfare, and the treasury needed another $29 billion more for donor-backed social wages.
Ukraine Counts on Beijing’s ‘Constructive Role’ as Sybiha Meets Chinese Ambassador
It had neither: In October, the government delayed $2.3 billion in development payments, and businesses went without value-added tax (VAT) refunds for a while.
Part of the problem also lies with Ukraine’s lawmakers, most of whom don’t see the worst of the war coming or the need to vote for reforms that will unlock the cash. The finance ministry has been sounding the alarm in finance for almost a year, since Ukraine signed the new $8.1 billion IMF program with benchmarks lawmakers must vote on.
The EU’s reform-tied Ukraine Facility also lists steps that parliament and the government have not adopted since 2025. The list deadlocked parliament from early 2026, as the government and lawmakers failed to agree until the treasury emptied. The EU, which had earlier accepted compromises, now refuses 2026 aid unless Ukraine implements the bills.
Now, Kyiv must find financing for 2026 and 2027 in under two months. The president and defense ministry team is negotiating weapons funding – one half of the financing – while the prime minister, finance ministry and central bank work on social spending, pensions and wounded businesses.
                                                                                                                                                                         (Chart by Olena Hrazhdan / Kyiv Post)                             
If lawmakers fail to vote for reforms, Ukraine may have nothing to pay for its survival and could resort to printing money and face protests.
“We will lose communications with international donors. The IMF program will be impossible to maintain with quantitative easing,” Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said at the tax committee meeting in September.
Ukraine printed money in 2022 and landed softly, but doing so again risks Argentinian or Venezuelan-style inflation.
If the IMF blocks a tranche over poor performance, Ukraine automatically loses the ability to attract aid from others, as the IMF’s green light signals that the country can be trusted. Defense needs make this funding a lifeline as Russia shows no desire to end the invasion.
But Ukraine’s delegation has options: reassure donors that the reforms have been voted on, and again negotiate the use of Russian assets.
To complete the mission, Kyiv must clear three quests: convince the IMF in Thailand, agree on funding with the EU, and push the Ukrainian parliament to do its one job.
Ukraine’s parliament and 2026 IMF Annual Meetings funding quests
For 2026, the EU told Ukraine it will receive the committed cash for its budget needs as parliament votes on the bills, a person familiar with the matter told Kyiv Post.
“In recent weeks, the IMF team has been in talks with various partners – primarily from the European Union – regarding the mobilization of additional funds to Ukraine. But Europeans gave a clear signal we need to fulfill the conditions necessary,” the person said.
Almost immediately after taking office, the new prime minister, Serhii Koretskiy, rushed to push through the reform decisions his predecessor, Yulia Svyrydenko, left undone.
Under Koretskiy, the government adopted six decisions that missed deadlines in 2025 and the first half of 2026. Eight Ukraine Facility steps and six of 12 Ukraine Support Loan conditions remain unmet, per the RRR4U monitoring, and President Volodymyr Zelensky still has not signed the digital-platform income tax bill, another IMF benchmark.
Finance Minister Marchenko did not attend the IMF’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand; instead, he kept a close eye on the lawmakers. When the state treasury became nearly empty, it partly worked: On the third attempt, they voted for an IMF benchmark scrapping the VAT exemption for parcels worth up to €150 ($174), and parliament began filling six of 11 Accounting Chamber seats.
                                                                                                                                                                         From left: IMF Alternate Executive Director Vladyslav Rashkovan, Deputy Minister of Finance Olha Zykova, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, National Bank of Ukraine Governor Andriy Pyshnyi and IMF European Department Director Mateusz Szczurek during a meeting on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. (Photo courtesy of Ukraine’s Ministry of Finance press service)                             
The mood was somber as delegations headed to Bangkok for the IMF Annual Meetings, but the last-minute vote reassured them.
“We came to Bangkok on a low, and we leave on a high. The Rada vote changed the mood. It showed once again that, against all odds, Ukraine continues to deliver on its reform agenda,” a well-informed source told Kyiv Post.
Before the meetings, the source was skeptical that the parties would arrive with any “significant headline announcements.”
Ukraine’s finance ministry is also happy.
“For our key partners, Ukraine’s performance is no longer in question. The discussion has now shifted to determining how to ensure and structure the necessary financing for 2027 in a sustainable and predictable manner,” Deputy Minister of Finance Olha Zykova told Kyiv Post.
                                                                                                                                                                         Ukraine’s finance ministry delegation at the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. From left: Deputy Ministers of Finance Yuriy Drahanchuk, Olha Zykova, Government Commissioner for Public Debt Management Yuriy Butsa and Finance Ministry press service staff. (Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Finance)                             
Kyiv Post still does not know whether Ukraine’s defense ministry shares that optimism. It did not answer Kyiv Post’s request on its $27 billion gap, but wrote that it freed up $354.5 million, 1.3% of the gap, by revising arms purchases.
Quest 2: Cash for 2027 and European partners
Immobilized Russian sovereign assets in the EU, amounting to €210 billion ($243.6 billion), remain key to Ukraine’s 2027 plan, despite earlier objections from Belgium.
Signed programs cover $20 billion for 2027, leaving $32.6 billion unfulfilled. Kyiv Post found that the EU has agreed to cover part of this, and Kyiv should find the rest outside the union.
“Depending on the final size of the EU contribution to cover the budgetary needs in 2027, we calculate the residual amount to be covered by other donors in the range of $10-15 billion,” the second source participating in the discussions told Kyiv Post.
“It’s important to obtain those financing assurances, including from the EU, by the next IMF review scheduled by the end of the year,” the person added.
                                                                                                                                                                         (Chart by Olena Hrazhdan / Kyiv Post)                             
Kyiv Post was told that Kyiv’s allies are doing “a lot of work on [a] technical level” to secure Ukraine’s 2027 funding needs, with further details remaining undisclosed.
One potential option is a second Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) loan backed by Russia’s frozen sovereign assets.
“The European Commission is working on developing various options,” a person familiar with the matter told Kyiv Post.
Partners seem less willing to confiscate the principal of the frozen assets, according to the source. And with the US, which took part in the earlier ERA Loan, also showing less enthusiasm, another option could be a new EU-backed Ukraine Support Loan, the person added.
“They can find the resource if they have the political will and simultaneously Ukrainian authorities deliver their promises,” the person said.
Negotiations should turn to specific financing assurances by early December, Zykova told Kyiv Post.
“The focus is on finding the right combination of support from the EU and our non-EU G7+ partners, while safeguarding Ukraine’s debt sustainability,” she said.
The second IMF review is planned for November, when Ukraine will again report on whether Kyiv did its homework, and partners will face another checkpoint on whether they did theirs amid a looming increase in Russian escalations across Ukraine in the months to come.

articles.title: Russian Ballistic Missile Attack Hits Kyiv Transport Facility, Injures Six
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv late Wednesday, Oct. 21, striking a transport infrastructure facility and damaging residential buildings and civilian businesses across the Ukrainian capital. At least six people were injured, four of whom were hospitalized.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported on Telegram that a transport infrastructure facility was hit in the Darnytskyi district, with emergency crews dispatched to the scene.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kyiv City Military Administration confirmed damage in a non-residential area of the district following the Russian strike.
Residential buildings and gas station damaged
The attack also caused damage across Kyiv’s Dniprovskyi district, where Russian missiles struck residential properties and civilian facilities.
Klitschko said a vehicle repair facility and a private residential building were directly hit, while debris struck another private home.
At another location in the same district, missile debris fell near a gas station, causing additional damage.
Klitschko initially reported one person hospitalized following the strikes before confirming that six people had been injured, including four requiring hospital treatment.
Kyiv targeted again after deadly Russian attacks
The latest assault began Wednesday evening, when explosions were heard across the capital following warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
Klitschko urged residents to remain in shelters as air defenses responded to the attack.
Italy Investigates Russia’s Possible Role in Violent Protests
The bombardment came amid a sustained wave of Russian strikes on Kyiv, targeting residential neighborhoods, energy infrastructure and transport facilities.
On Oct. 20, Russian attacks killed one person and injured 21 others in the capital, according to city authorities. Twelve of the injured were hospitalized, including three in serious condition.
Early Wednesday, Russian drones also struck a 24-story apartment building in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district, killing two people and injuring two others.

articles.title: MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine
articles.body:
MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal has challenged Elon Musk’s denials over alleged restrictions on satellite services used for Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia. The outlet has cited anonymous White House sources who have claimed that the SpaceX founder and Starlink owner had personally ordered restricting the service.
Ukrainian officials last week claimed that SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service and its military-grade version, Starshield, which Kiev uses for frontline drone operations, stopped working on drones traveling faster than 160 kph (100 mph). Neither Starlink nor SpaceX has publicly acknowledged a technical “signal or service failure,” leaving the questions of whether an actual service restriction took place, and if so what could have caused it, unconfirmed.
What has Ukraine claimed about Starshield?
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky initially claimed, without evidence, that Kiev had been told “technical malfunctions” had caused a service slowdown. He later shifted the blame to Washington. On NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday Zelensky claimed, again without citing evidence nor being asked to provide it, that an order had come from the US government. According to Zelensky, Kiev had even secretly despatched cars to the EU, where they could drive "legally" at 180kph (110mph) where tests allegedly surfaced discrepancies in Starlink performance between the EU and Ukraine.
What has Musk said about Starshield?
Musk has categorically denied that he instructed SpaceX to restrict either service, nor has he confirmed that any restriction or slowdown took place.
The WSJ cited anonymous sources who contradicted him, alleging on Tuesday that he personally ordered speed limits on Ukrainian hardware connected to the satellite network.
Even the WSJ's sources accounts differed. Some claimed that Musk acted unilaterally; others said he consulted senior administration officials, including President Donald Trump, before making the decision. The outlet also claimed that SpaceX representatives contacted the White House to coordinate their accounts of whether the restrictions had been agreed on with the administration.
What has the US government said about Starshield?
Musk earlier insisted that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, meaning any speed or usage restrictions are determined by the US military and ultimately Trump – who denied that he ordered the restrictions, though he said on Monday he “would like to find out” who did. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent both said the administration was not behind the restrictions, with Bessent rebuking Zelensky for making “reckless” allegations.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rejected the claims. Questioned about the allegation during a visit to India on Wednesday, he warned Kiev against escalating the dispute, saying Ukraine “would not exist” as a sovereign state without US support.
Relations between Zelensky and Washington have effectively collapsed in recent weeks over sanctions on Russia and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Both Musk and Trump have sharply criticized Ukraine’s attacks on Russian diesel refineries, blaming them for global fuel shortages and soaring prices at the pump.
Speaking at the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump warned Zelensky that he is “going to have to want to make a deal.” He also criticized the cost of supporting Kiev, saying the US has received “absolutely nothing back” except “grief, death and tremendous monetary loss.”
What did Kiev say about Starshield?
Despite Zelensky’s evidence-free assertions and there being no record in the public sphere to support it, the Western press and Ukrainian diplomats are echoing the claims regardless. Ukraine’s ambassador in Washington, Denis Senik, said on Tuesday that Kiev is still “waiting for the official response from contacts with the Pentagon and SpaceX” to understand what happened.
What did the Kremlin say about Starshield?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last week that Moscow is unaware of the reported Starlink restrictions, but stressed that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.” Moscow has condemned Western military assistance for Kiev, arguing that it only prolongs the conflict and obstructs peace efforts.
Is there any proof Starshield was slowed down?
There is no proof on the public record or in the public domain that the Starshield was affected. The only suggestions supporting the idea such an incident took place are Vladimir Zelensky's uncontested claim that Ukrainians sent cars to the EU with Starlink terminals to compare data and the claims of an anonymous Ukrainian officer who told German media giant Axel Springer's Global Reporter's Network, seemingly during the alleged service restriction, that all operations were on hold.

articles.title: Lockheed Martin Offers Ukraine Its Own Version of F-16
articles.body:
Lockheed Martin is considering developing a specialized version of the F-16 fighter jet tailored to Ukraine’s needs.
Company sources told about this to The Defence Blog.
One option under consideration is a new F-16 variant with an extended range and a more advanced radar.
This would allow pilots to detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles earlier than the radars on Ukraine’s current aircraft can.
The company is also considering integrating European weapons into the fighter’s onboard systems, including guided aerial bombs and cruise missiles.
This would expand the range of weapons available to Ukrainian F-16s.
According to the sources, no concrete negotiations on developing a new variant are underway yet.
At the same time, Ukraine is interested in an affordable, versatile fighter that its pilots have already mastered in combat.
The sources told the media outlet that Lockheed Martin expects to pursue numerous joint projects with Ukraine.
The sources did not specify the cost of a specialized Ukrainian variant, the possible number of aircraft under the program, or which European weapons the company would prioritize for integration.
Implementing such a program would require approval from Washington. Until that approval is obtained, the initiative remains at an early stage.
Militarnyi previously reported that Ukraine’s industrial partners had accelerated F-16 fighter jet repairs due to the aircraft’s intensive operational use.

articles.title: Netanyahu ‘completely lacks legitimacy’ to launch new war ahead of elections: Opposition leader Golan
articles.body:
Yair Golan, leader of Israel’s opposition Democrats party, said Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “completely lacks the legitimacy” to launch a war ahead of Oct. 27 legislative elections, Anadolu reports.
His remarks came after The Financial Times reported that US President Donald Trump had rejected Netanyahu’s plan to strike infrastructure and nuclear facilities in Iran, a military campaign that was reportedly set to begin on Oct. 10.
Trump opposes any military escalation ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm congressional elections in the US, fearing negative repercussions for the Republican Party’s electoral prospects, according to the report.
Golan, also a former deputy chief of staff of the Israeli army, said in a post on US social media platform X: “Netanyahu is a sick and weak leader clinging to power by force, willing to put Israel’s security at risk to save himself.”
The upcoming general election is seen as crucial to Netanyahu’s political future.
He is standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud, and breach of trust, which could result in imprisonment if he is convicted.
Golan further criticized Netanyahu, saying he “completely lacks the legitimacy to drag Israel into another military campaign, driven by personal and political calculations, on the eve of the election.”
Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court over war crimes in the Gaza Strip since 2023, has headed the current government since late 2022.
READ: Netanyahu, opposition blocs tied as 55% back unity government if election inconclusive: Poll
Since October 2023, Israel has launched a genocidal war in Gaza.
It has also waged wars against Lebanon and Iran, carried out airstrikes on Yemen and Qatar, and conducted near-daily ground incursions into Syria.
Golan called on Israeli army’s Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and security establishment leaders to “oppose any military action intended to serve personal interests under the pretext of security needs,” while also urging voters to go to the polls to “save Israel from this dangerous government.”
Separately, Gadi Eisenkot, head of the opposition Yashar party, said Netanyahu’s claim of destroying Iranian nuclear bombs was “an outright lie.”
“Iran has never possessed nuclear bombs,” Eisenkot said in remarks carried by Israel’s public broadcaster KAN, arguing that he sees “no direct and immediate threat that requires action.”
Eisenkot is widely viewed as the opposition figure with the strongest potential to challenge Netanyahu in the upcoming elections.
A Channel 12 poll released Monday found that 45% of respondents considered Eisenkot better suited to serve as prime minister, compared with 33% for Netanyahu, widening Eisenkot’s lead to 12 percentage points from 10 in the previous survey.
However, polls generally suggest that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is likely to secure a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of another election unless one side agrees to form a coalition with Palestinian parties in Israel.
In a separate statement on X, the Israeli military said Wednesday that its personnel had begun early voting, including troops stationed in occupied territories in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.

articles.title: “Your Peace Is Capitulation”: Protesters Rally in Sofia Against Government’s "Russia Policy"
articles.body:
Bulgaria Issues Over 13,000 Seasonal Work Permits to Non-EU Nationals
Bulgaria had issued more than 13,000 seasonal work permits to non-EU nationals by July 10, as businesses increasingly rely on foreign workers to fill staffing gaps
A protest against the government's response to security developments in the Black Sea took place in central Sofia, with demonstrators demanding a stronger defense policy and closer coordination with Bulgaria's EU and NATO allies.
The demonstration, held under the slogan "Your 'Peace' Is Capitulation! Your 'Diplomacy' Is Isolation!", was organized through social media and focused on national security, defense policy, and Bulgaria's relations with its European and Euro-Atlantic partners. Participants criticized the country's leadership for its response to events in the Black Sea and called for a clear position and concrete measures to protect Bulgaria.
The organizers cited attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, casualties, and incidents in which Russian drones came dangerously close to Bulgaria's borders. They argued that these developments required a consistent defense policy and closer cooperation with allies in the European Union and NATO.
"How much longer will we pretend not to see what is happening right at our doorstep?" the organizers asked, stressing that diplomatic efforts should not weaken Bulgaria's defense capabilities. They added: "Illusions do not save lives. Silence is not a strategy."
Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev said public discontent stemmed primarily from what he described as an inadequate response by the government and the president. He argued that the authorities' refusal to identify the party responsible for actions threatening Bulgaria's security and its citizens was preventing the adoption of necessary measures.
“When discussing a response in this crisis situation, we must act based on the available information. As of now, all available information points to the unequivocal conclusion that the perpetrator of the attacks is Russia - the Russian Federation,” Tagarev told Bulgarian media BGNES.
He warned that Russian provocations extended beyond NATO's eastern flank, affecting other European countries, including Germany, Denmark, and Ireland. According to Tagarev, Moscow sought to frighten European societies and weaken public support for Ukraine. He said Ukraine would struggle severely to resist Russian aggression without European assistance.
Tagarev maintained that achieving a lasting and just peace required European and democratic countries to work together to help Ukraine stop Russia's aggression on its territory, thereby preventing further threats to European security.
Journalist Georgi Angelov also called on Bulgarian authorities to adopt a firm position on developments in the Black Sea, pointing to Poland and Romania as examples of how states should respond.
"It is clear who is carrying out the attacks, it is the Russians, and this is being stated explicitly," Angelov said.
He criticized Bulgarian journalism for what he described as self-censorship, fear, and insufficient professional training among some media workers. While distinguishing the current media environment from the censorship imposed under communist rule, he argued that freedom of speech could coexist with implicit pressure and self-restraint.
"I call this self-censorship. Either they do not tell the truth, they do not dare to tell the truth, or they do not know the truth," Angelov said.
He explained that he had joined the protest because he opposed the policies of Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, describing their relationship as a "terrible tandem."
Addressing demonstrators later, Angelov called for Russia to withdraw all its generals from Bulgaria, as he said it had done after the Unification. He accused those in power of being afraid to identify Russia as the aggressor and of instead labeling protesters warmongers. He urged voters to make careful choices in the upcoming elections to prevent Bulgaria from following a path similar to Hungary under Viktor Orbán.
The demonstration outside the Presidency remained peaceful despite a heavy police presence, including heavily armed officers. Protesters chanted "Resignation!" and held signs criticizing Radev's position.
Several participants also explained their views to BGNES. Mihail Donchev said the demonstrators supported peace but rejected what he called "Russian peace." He argued that a just settlement should respect the right of the attacked party to defend itself and should not involve its public humiliation.
Bozhidar Penchev said the government's position should be aligned with NATO's. He argued that Russia was the country benefiting from the Black Sea becoming a dangerous economic zone.
Aleksandar Krastev accused Radev of taking contradictory positions in Bulgaria and before European institutions. He also criticized the lack of a clear government stance and delays in joining various initiatives with partner countries.
"No one here wants Bulgaria to become part of the conflict. We want Bulgaria to act just as our allies in NATO and the EU do," Krastev said, adding that Ukraine should receive support until the very end to secure a just peace.
Earlier in the day, young doctors held a separate demonstration outside the Ministry of Health, demanding reforms, improved working conditions, and pay that would allow them to remain in Bulgaria and develop their careers there. Teacher Ivan Dzhenezov supported the initiative, calling for greater solidarity between universities and students. The two protests addressed different concerns, with one focused on national security and defense and the other on working conditions and professional opportunities in health care. Opposition representatives also participated in the demonstrations.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev had accused those planning the protest outside the Presidency of seeking to draw Bulgaria into the war and restore Boyko Borissov and Delyan Peevski to power.
"The organizers' agenda is becoming increasingly clear: to resurrect the 'assembly' [the governing coalition], to whitewash Borissov and Peevski, and to return to power alongside them—since they cannot do so on their own. They want to drag us into the war and have Asen Vassilev draft the budget - which would be the final blow for us," Radev said.
Two demonstrations had been announced for the capital that day. The first, organized by the young doctors' "Future in Bulgaria" initiative, was scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. outside the Ministry of Health before proceeding toward the National Assembly. The second, referred to by Radev, was scheduled for 6:30 p.m. outside the Presidency under the slogan "Your 'peace' is capitulation! Your 'diplomacy' is isolation! How much longer will we pretend not to see what is happening right at our doorstep?"
Among the organizers were former Environment and Water Minister Borislav Sandov, former members of parliament Lena Borislavova and Metodi Andreev, former ambassador to Moscow Iliyan Vasilev, economist Evgeni Kanev, and representatives of the Justice for Everyone initiative.
Radev attributed growing discontent among European citizens to several factors, including uncontrolled migration, failed integration, the Green Deal, deindustrialization, and job losses.
"But there is another important factor, which I have been speaking about for a long time: the war in Ukraine is draining our economic systems, leading to social tension and political instability - and that is what we are seeing right now. It will become increasingly difficult to provide a political answer as to why the prosperity of European citizens is being poured into this war, instead of being used to address their own problems," Radev said.
He argued that Bulgaria could not be expected to contribute to the 70 billion in European aid for Ukraine and called for a diplomatic solution to the war.
Radev also addressed the investigation into the attack on the ship Chelsea-3, saying a chemical analysis would be carried out to establish which type of explosive substance had been used.
