articles.title: German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
articles.body:
German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
A German sniper who deserted the Ukrainian military after failing to receive a promised payment has been detained by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), the agency announced on Wednesday.
In footage released by the agency, the man said he had served with German forces in Afghanistan between 2004 and 2010, took part in fighting in Somalia from 2006 to 2008, and later fought as a mercenary in Syria between 2008 and 2010.
The former Bundeswehr soldier said he then served as a sniper with Ukraine’s 25th Territorial Defense Battalion near Donetsk between 2016 and 2018, alongside fighters mainly from Britain and Georgia.
He later moved to Switzerland before returning to Ukraine in November 2025 to sign another three-year military contract the following month. The man said he held the rank of corporal and served as a sniper.
“After signing the contract, I was promised a payment of 100,000 hryvnias ($2,200). However, I did not receive this money and was forced to flee the Ukrainian armed forces,” he said in the testimony.
The FSB released copies of the German national’s military documents and contracts, with his identity concealed, as well as photographs showing him alongside other fighters. The agency said he could face criminal charges for mercenary activity under Russian law.
The detention comes a week after the FSB apprehended Swedish national Freddy Mikael Stalkrantz Lindholm in Russia’s Pskov Region. According to the agency, he crossed the border illegally to carry out sabotage and terrorist attacks on Russian military facilities, posing as a prospective recruit for the Russian Army.
Lindholm previously commanded a drone unit in Ukraine’s Aidar battalion, which Russia has designated a terrorist organization. He faces charges of illegally crossing the border, while investigators are considering additional charges related to terrorism and mercenary activity.
US investigators have also reportedly uncovered a scheme in which Mexican drug cartels sent their members to Ukraine to gain battlefield experience and paid officials close to Vladimir Zelensky for their “training,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on Tuesday.
Kiev has increasingly turned to foreign fighters as its military struggles with manpower shortages, draft evasion, and desertion. In March, then-Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov identified the recruitment of more foreigners as one of the measures aimed at tackling Ukraine’s mobilization crisis.
At least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have fought for Kiev since 2022, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova told the OSCE Forum for Security Co-operation earlier this month, saying most came from the US, UK, Canada, and Georgia.
Moscow has repeatedly pursued criminal cases against foreign fighters fighting for Kiev, including prosecutions in absentia, and has warned that mercenaries are not entitled to prisoner-of-war protections under the Geneva Conventions.

articles.title: Ukraine and Norway Race to Test FREYJA Ballistic Missile Interceptor by Year’s End
articles.body:
- Category

Ukraine and Norway Race to Test FREYJA Ballistic Missile Interceptor by Year’s End
Ukraine and Norway are accelerating development of the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile defense program, with initial components already showing progress and the first tests targeted for the end of 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the development on October 21 following a meeting with Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik, Kongsberg CEO Eirik Lie, and representatives of the Norwegian defense company.
According to Zelenskyy, Norway is actively participating in the European FREYJA program, which aims to develop new capabilities for intercepting ballistic missile threats.
The Ukrainian president confirmed that work on individual elements of the system has already produced initial results. During the meeting, Ukrainian and Norwegian officials identified areas where development could be accelerated to begin testing before the end of the year.
Kongsberg, one of Norway’s leading defense manufacturers, produces the NASAMS air defense system, which Ukraine currently operates to protect cities and critical infrastructure against Russian missile and drone attacks.
The discussions also addressed additional military assistance from Norway. Zelenskyy said Ukraine expects new defense support packages to arrive as early as November, although he did not specify their contents.
Another priority was the development of new satellite communications capabilities for Ukraine’s Defense Forces. Zelenskyy said the initiative would involve additional international partners with the necessary technological resources.
Earlier, Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point upgraded its FP-7.x Freyja interceptor missile with a dual-mode infrared and radar seeker. Developed as part of the European FREYJA program, the missile is designed to counter ballistic threats, including Russia’s Iskander-class missiles, while offering a lower-cost alternative to US-made Patriot interceptors.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Starshield Limits Remain as US Restores Missile Intelligence Sharing
articles.body:

Zelenskyy Says Starshield Limits Remain as US Restores Missile Intelligence Sharing
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Starlink and Starshield services used by Ukrainian forces remain restricted, although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has promised to work on resolving the issue, Fox News reported on October 21.
“Regarding Starlink and Starshield: they are still restricted, but the secretary of state told me that he will work with his team to unblock this issue,” Zelenskyy stated in an interview with Fox News.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Hegseth also addressed the Starshield restrictions, stating that the Pentagon had not ordered any reduction in support for Ukraine. “We haven’t pulled anything back,” he stated, adding that any restrictions were tied to Starlink’s terms of service rather than a US directive.
Zelenskyy also confirmed that the US had restored intelligence sharing with Ukraine, including information about Russian ballistic missile launches.
The restrictions on Starshield terminals emerged overnight on October 14, when SpaceX imposed new speed limits in Ukraine without advance warning.
The restrictions were reportedly imposed directly by Elon Musk. The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the October 14 Starshield slowdown, disrupting Ukrainian drone and interceptor operations, even though he later wrote that speed and usage limits were controlled by the US military and ultimately the president.
The terminals stopped functioning at speeds above roughly 160 kilometers per hour, disrupting systems used by Ukrainian forces to intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed-type drones.

articles.title: Ukraine’s interceptor crews destroyed thousands of Russian aerial targets during Vivaldi. Jet-powered Shaheds remain a challenge
articles.body:
The commander of an interceptor battalion in Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps said his unit destroyed several thousand Russian aerial targets during Operation Vivaldi, ArmyInform, the Defense Ministry’s news agency, reported on 21 October.
Operation Vivaldi is a Ukrainian counteroffensive north of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast, where the 3rd Army Corps has reported liberating settlements. In its third phase, Ukrainian forces reclaimed five settlements and expanded their gains to 176 square kilometers. Strikes on Russian logistics and electronic warfare likely neutralized Russia’s drone defenses before Ukraine sent in armor, the Institute for the Study of War assessed.
The commander, who uses the callsign “Betsyk,” leads the interceptor battalion of the 1030th Anti-Aircraft Missile-Artillery Regiment “Aquila,” part of the 3rd Army Corps. He said Russian forces deployed large numbers of reconnaissance drones to locate Ukrainian positions after the corps began advancing.
Betsyk named Zala, Orlan, Supercam, Merlin, and Knyaz Veshchiy Oleg among the reconnaissance drones used by Russian forces.
Russia also brought in reinforcements and units operating strike drones, including first-person-view (FPV) quadcopters, Molniya fixed-wing FPV drones, and Lancet crews, he said. At one stage, Russian forces deployed crews from their Rubicon drone unit to disrupt the advance, but the move did not change the situation.
Ukraine retook Kolodiazi north of Lyman as its drones hit 200-plus Russian vehicles in Operation Vivaldi’s last phase, Ukrainian drone officer says
Betsyk said his battalion’s work deprived Russian forces of the ability to strike Ukrainian troops and track their movements.
Jet-powered Shaheds: speed is the main challenge
The regiment also works against Russian strike drones heading for targets behind the front line. Betsyk said interceptor crews had destroyed some jet-powered drones, but not in significant numbers.
The main difficulty is speed, he said. Interceptor drones need to reach 500–600 km/h to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, according to Betsyk.
For now, the regiment mainly uses conventional air-defense systems against these targets: self-propelled anti-aircraft systems, surface-to-air missile systems, and portable surface-to-air missile systems. Betsyk said these systems were historically designed to engage jet-powered targets.
He compared the current challenge with the early use of piston-powered Shaheds. Those drones initially posed a serious threat but later became easier for Ukrainian air defenses to counter. Russia has largely stopped using piston-powered Shaheds on most fronts since summer, he said, but continues to use piston-powered Gerbera drones, which are relatively cheap and can partly exhaust Ukrainian air defenses. The main drones Russian forces use now are jet-powered Shaheds, he said.
Betsyk expects Russian forces to adapt if Ukraine fields effective interceptors against jet-powered drones. They will seek ways to evade the interceptors, increase speed, improve navigation, and change their tactics, he said. However, he added that the battalion had not observed a major evolution so far and did not expect the drones’ speed to double.
What the corps says Vivaldi achieved
Separately, 3rd Army Corps commander Andrii Biletskyi said Ukrainian forces retook 277 square kilometers and 16 settlements during Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Biletskyi also said Russian losses exceeded 8,000 personnel, according to ArmyInform. These figures are Ukrainian claims and have not been independently verified.
Read also

- Russia’s jet drones fly near 600 km/h now. Ukraine is building simulators for the 900 km/h ones it expects next
- Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles rock Kyiv in late-night attack, injuring 6
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russian ballistic missiles struck multiple locations in Kyiv on the night of Oct. 21-22, injuring six people as explosions rocked the city.
At around 2 a.m. local time on Oct. 22, Russian attacks on Kyiv continued, filling the sky with the sounds of explosions.
In the Dniprovsky district, a car service station and a private residential building were damaged in the attack late on Oct. 21, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
"In the same district, debris also hit another private residential building," Klitschko said. "There may be people trapped under the rubble."
In the Darnitsky district, also on the left bank of the Dnipro River that cuts through the city of 3 million, missiles hit near a transportation infrastructure facility.
"I was at home, in my private house," said Vladyslav, a resident of Kyiv living near one of the strikes. "When the explosion happened, our windows were blown out. Then we saw a terrifying glow outside; we ran out and saw a house on fire, and heard people screaming. Fortunately, we managed to rescue a man and his wife who were inside the burning house. It's a stroke of luck that neighbors were nearby to help save these people."
Ballistic missiles again targeted Kyiv at around 3:00 a.m. local time, with at least 13 explosions rocking the city in less than eight minutes, the Kyiv Independent's Chris York said.
Some journalists also reported power and wifi outages in parts of the city before another round of explosions set off at around 3:34 a.m.
Following the series of explosions, the Kyiv City Military Administration said that a building housing a medical facility was damaged in the city's Pecherskyi district.
The latest attack comes as Russian forces continue to intensify missile and drone campaigns against Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin.
Earlier on Oct. 21, a Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed at least two people and injured two others in the morning.
On Oct. 20, Russian drones repeatedly struck Kyiv, damaging a hospital in Solomyanskyi District and another medical facility in Holosiivskyi District, injuring 12 people, according to local authorities. That morning, three people were killed, and four people were injured after a Russian drone struck early-morning commuter traffic.
The U.N. Human Rights Office reported in early October that an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or injured every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, a 55% increase from the same period in 2025.
The strikes on Kyiv on the night of Oct. 21 came after shows of support for trilateral peace negotiations by both President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"We hope that Russia—which has stated many times that it is ready for a meeting in one format or another—will follow through," Zelensky said.
As Kyiv was under red alert from the incoming ballistic missiles late on Oct. 21, around the world in Washington, D.C., U.S. President Donald Trump said that a deal to "settle the war" is "maybe now the closest we've been," in a roundtable conference.

articles.title: Poland reportedly suspends major arms shipment to Ukraine over regional tribute to Ukrainian Insurgent Army, whose fighters took part in WWII massacres of Poles
articles.body:
Poland reportedly suspends major arms shipment to Ukraine over regional tribute to Ukrainian Insurgent Army, whose fighters took part in WWII massacres of Poles
Poland has suspended delivery of a large weapons package to Ukraine over the Lviv Regional Council’s decision to declare 2027 the year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a source told the news outlet RBC Ukraine.
Lviv Regional Council members voted at an October 20 plenary session to declare 2027 the year of the UPA, its commander Roman Shukhevych, and Ukrainian political figure Oleh Olzhych.
The source told RBC Ukraine that the Lviv regional authorities had “managed” to hold the vote just as Poland was preparing to send Ukraine a large military aid package. “Their irresponsible actions have now put delivery of this package on hold. Intensive efforts are underway through back channels to resolve a problem that was created out of nothing,” the source said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the Lviv Regional Council’s decision “unwise” and said it “harms Ukraine itself.” Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the decision unacceptable, saying it “deepens divisions” between the two peoples. “The Ukrainian authorities must distance themselves from this position,” he said.
Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said Ukraine had assured Poland that the Lviv Regional Council’s decision would not take effect. He said the resolution had disappeared from the council’s website after Poland intervened.
The Lviv Regional Council’s Facebook post announcing the year of the UPA is now unavailable.
Issues surrounding the Ukrainian Insurgent Army regularly strain relations between Poland and Ukraine. The most recent such dispute arose in the spring of 2026, when Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree awarding the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA” to the Separate Special Operations Center North, part of the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ Special Operations Forces. The decision drew sharp criticism in Poland because UPA fighters took part in the Volhynia massacres of 1943–1944, in which an estimated 30,000 to 60,000 Poles and 20,000 to 30,000 Ukrainians were killed. After Poland condemned the decision, Zelensky promised to open the archives on the Volhynia massacres.

articles.title: How Egypt's Saudi pledge aims to curb Israel's Gulf ambitions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Egypt's Saudi pledge aims to curb Israel's Gulf ambitions
Egypt, a regional military power, has pledged to provide all forms of assistance to defend Saudi Arabia amid escalating Houthi attacks from Yemen, in a move aimed at maintaining its strategic position in the Gulf.
But analysts view another geopolitical objective behind the Egyptian support for Riyadh: countering Israel’s bid to play a security role in a region vital to Cairo’s political and economic interests.
On 17 October, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt would take any necessary measures to protect Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requested assistance. He called an emergency parliamentary session to authorise possible troop deployment.
The following day, the National Defence Council, Egypt’s top security body, pledged to provide all necessary and possible support to safeguard Saudi Arabia’s security, stability, and territorial integrity.
The Egyptian pledge came after US President Donald Trump said on 16 October that Israel had been helping Saudi Arabia counter Houthi attacks from Yemen and suggested Riyadh should accept further Israeli assistance.
It followed Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Cairo last month to seek support against the Iran-backed Houthis. The visit highlighted the importance of Egyptian-Saudi coordination on issues affecting the Red Sea and wider regional stability.
For Cairo, which has longstanding strategic ties with Riyadh, the prospect of Israel becoming a more prominent security partner for the kingdom adds urgency to its efforts to reinforce its role in regional security.
“Egypt’s interest lies in doing everything possible to strengthen its ties with Saudi Arabia, or at least to ensure that its relationship with Riyadh is closer than Israel’s,” Ahmed Aboudouh, an associate fellow at Chatham House in London, told The New Arab.
Strengthening ties with Saudi Arabia offers Egypt significant economic and geopolitical benefits as Cairo seeks foreign investment, financial support, and foreign currency. The kingdom is also important for millions of Egyptians working there, whose remittances provide a vital source of foreign currency.
Closer coordination with Riyadh also helps Egypt protect its interests in the Red Sea, particularly shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key route to the Suez Canal and a major source of revenue for Cairo.
During Trump’s first term, the US brokered the Abraham Accords in 2020 to normalise relations between Israel and Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia’s neighbours, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Bahrain, allowing Tel Aviv to expand its economic, diplomatic, and security partnerships in the Gulf.
The American president has also pushed for normalising ties between Saudi Arabia and Israel, but Riyadh insists that any normalisation depends on resolving the Palestinian issue, including the establishment of a Palestinian state.
If Riyadh accepts any Israeli assistance against Houthi attacks, cooperation in areas such as intelligence sharing and air defence could expand, potentially giving Israel a greater role in Gulf security.
For Egypt, that possibility raises concerns about a changing regional balance in which Israel could become a more influential security partner for Arab states traditionally linked to Cairo.
Cairo's bid to keep Israel at bay
“Egypt would oppose any attempt by Israel to become a player in the Arab world’s collective security, regardless of who was involved, and Saudi Arabia would certainly stand with Cairo. This means keeping Israel out of regional military and intelligence cooperation,” Egyptian military expert Samir Ragheb told The New Arab.
Egypt was the first Arab country to sign a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, following decades of conflict and several wars, but their relations have remained largely cold despite formal diplomatic ties.
The relationship has been marked by mutual distrust, periodic tensions, and regional competition, particularly over Gaza and broader Middle East security arrangements.
Egyptian political analyst Mokhtar Ghobashi said Egypt’s pledge to defend Saudi Arabia could deter Israel from seeking a security role in the Gulf.
“Relying on Israel as a security guarantor for a country in the Arab world, amid divisions and conflicts between Arab states, is an extremely dangerous proposition,” he told The New Arab.
Since the 2020 Abraham Accords, security cooperation between Israel and some Gulf states has expanded, including arms sales and coordination on air and missile defence amid shared concerns over Iran.
Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia reflects its interest in preserving its regional influence and maintaining a central role in shaping the security arrangements in the Middle East.
Cairo could face greater competition for influence if Riyadh turns to Israel for certain defence capabilities. While this would not necessarily weaken Egyptian-Saudi relations, it could reduce Egypt’s role in shaping the kingdom’s security policy.
The implications extend beyond bilateral relations. Closer security ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia could give Tel Aviv a greater role in shaping regional responses to threats, from Yemen’s Houthis to Iran.
Protecting Egypt's strategic interests
Red Sea security is another concern for Cairo. A broader Israeli security role in the Gulf could give Tel Aviv greater influence over decisions affecting the Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime corridor central to Egypt’s national interests.
Aboudouh said another objective behind Egypt’s pledge to defend Saudi Arabia is to protect its strategic interests in the Red Sea and around Bab el-Mandeb.
“Egyptian officials may have concluded that expanding the country’s regional role is now crucial to protecting maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait against any Houthi attempt to exploit a conflict with Saudi Arabia to disrupt shipping, as they have done in the past,” he told The New Arab.
Egypt has been hard-hit by regional instability following Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip and Houthi attacks on shipping in the Red Sea since 2023, losing an estimated around $20 billion in Suez Canal revenues.
Sisi framed Egypt’s potential role in Saudi Arabia as defensive, saying Cairo had no intention of attacking any party but was prepared to defend Saudi Arabia if requested. “We do not want to fight or attack anyone. We will only defend Saudi Arabia,” he said.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen against the Houthis in 2015, but its role remained limited. A deeper commitment now could expose Cairo to a costly conflict, particularly if operations extend beyond the defence of Saudi territory.
It could also strain Egypt’s resources and increase its exposure to instability along the Red Sea.
The extent and form of any Egyptian assistance will therefore be crucial. Intelligence-sharing, logistical support and maritime security cooperation would carry different risks from deploying troops to Yemen.
Cairo may seek to bolster Saudi Arabia’s defences while avoiding involvement in an open-ended conflict.
Mohamed Sabry is an Egyptian journalist based in Cairo with over two decades of experience covering Egypt, regional politics, foreign policy, and diplomacy. His work has appeared in Al-Monitor and InsideOver
Follow him on X: @MohamedSabry079

articles.title: U.S. Navy taps portable reactor to power Indiana base
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy selected Radiant to install a 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program.
- The Department of War wants the Navy’s first shore-based microreactor operating at Crane no later than September 2028.
The U.S. Navy has selected Radiant to install its Kaleidos nuclear microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana, putting a commercial company in charge of the service’s first shore-based advanced reactor, which the Department of War wants running no later than September 2028.
Radiant announced the selection on Oct. 20, about six weeks after the Department of War named Crane as the site for the Navy’s first microreactor without saying which vendor would build it.
Kaleidos is a factory-built reactor that produces 1 megawatt of electricity and is designed to be moved by truck, ship or aircraft and set up at a customer’s site without cooling water, major excavation or extensive construction. Each unit runs for up to five years before it needs refueling, over a planned service life of 20 years, and at Crane it is meant to keep power flowing to the base independently of the regional grid, which matters for an installation where the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division, works on microelectronics, high-voltage systems and weapons.
The reactor will be installed under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program, the Pentagon effort to put commercially owned and operated microreactors on military bases so they can keep critical facilities running through grid outages. Before it reaches Crane, the project still has to move through design refinement, prototype testing, environmental review, site preparation and coordination with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, with technical support from the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, the organization that runs the reactors on the Navy’s carriers and submarines.
“The Janus Program was built from day one to deliver real, reliable hardware and systems to solve energy resilience challenges across all of the Services,” said Dr. Jeff Waksman, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment. “We are excited to partner with the Navy to place a Janus reactor at NWS Crane, and by doing so to deliver the state of Indiana its first advanced microreactor.”
Crane is the second military base Radiant has lined up this year under Janus. In August, the U.S. Army awarded contracts worth up to $2.2 billion to five reactor makers, with Radiant receiving the largest share, up to $750 million to deploy 15 Kaleidos units by 2030, as we reported, starting with three reactors at Fort Benning in Georgia that will back up Lawson Army Airfield and other critical facilities, we reported in September. The company also has a deal with the Defense Innovation Unit and the Department of the Air Force to deliver a Kaleidos unit by 2028, and it now says it is the only nuclear company working with the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy and U.S. Air Force at once.
“Our installations are foundational warfighting platforms and ensuring their resilience is essential to supporting the Fleet,” said Vice Adm. Brad Collins, Commander, Navy Installations Command. “By investing in advanced capabilities like this microreactor at Crane, we are providing our Shore infrastructure with the resources needed to sustain the mission and empower our warfighters.”
Radiant has not yet proven the design at full scale, and the reactor is now going through a year-long test campaign at the Idaho National Laboratory’s DOME facility, where the Department of Energy gave the company exclusive access after a competitive selection. The company says the test uses the same reactor design and the same type of fresh fuel that will go to military customers, running at full power for an extended period to show the performance and reliability needed before deployment.
The Navy brings decades of reactor experience to the project, since the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, founded in 1948, has logged more than 7,500 reactor-years of operation and over 171 million miles under nuclear power without a reactor accident.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian heavy rocket launcher near Black Sea coast
articles.body:
- Ukraine’s Prymary drone unit destroyed a Russian Tornado-S rocket launcher near Skadovsk in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting it with several kamikaze drones.
- OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to Ulyanivka, while HUR said the unit also hit a Buk-M3, an Orion drone and four radars.
Ukrainian drones have destroyed a Russian 9K515 Tornado-S heavy multiple launch rocket system in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting the launcher with several different kamikaze drones in succession in a strike carried out by the Prymary unit of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR), which released the footage on Oct. 20.
OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to the village of Ulyanivka just outside Skadovsk, at coordinates 46.189524, 32.964916, which places the launcher close to the Black Sea coast and well behind the Dnipro River front line.
The video shows the Tornado-S being struck by drones of different types one after another, a method Ukrainian operators use against high-value vehicles so that a second or third drone can finish off a target that survives the first hit before the crew can drive it away. HUR did not give the exact date of the strike, saying only that it took place over the past month, and Russia has not commented on the loss.
The Tornado-S is one of the most valuable launchers in Russia’s rocket artillery, since it is a modernized version of the Soviet 9A52 Smerch that fires 300 mm (11.8-inch) rockets from a 12-tube launcher mounted on an eight-wheeled Kamaz truck. Built by NPO Splav in Tula, part of the state-owned Rostec group, the system uses digital fire control and GLONASS satellite navigation so its three-person crew can prepare and fire a full salvo without leaving the cab, and its guided rockets can reach targets up to 120 km (75 miles) away.
That range lets Russian crews fire on Ukrainian cities from deep inside occupied territory, and in the south the system has repeatedly been used against Kherson and other towns along the Dnipro from positions in the occupied part of the region. Ukrainian units put a high price on each launcher they destroy, and after a drone strike on a Tornado-S in the Huliaipole sector in July, the Pomsta Border Guard Brigade estimated the vehicle’s value at more than $15 million.
The Skadovsk strike is the latest in a series of Tornado-S losses this year as Ukrainian drones reach further behind Russian lines. In February, the Ptahi unit of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces destroyed a launcher in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast with FP-2 strike drones guided by reconnaissance drones, we reported at the time, and in March a long-range Fire Point drone hit three Tornado-S launchers and a transport-loader near Karakul in occupied Crimea, as we reported. Two more launchers were hit near Melitopol within a few days in late April, followed by the July strike in the Huliaipole sector.
“Big names, formidable specifications and the millions invested in military equipment do not guarantee the occupiers’ immunity,” Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said in its statement.
The Tornado-S was the centerpiece of a wider monthly report from Prymary, which HUR said also hit a Buk-M3 air defense system, an Orion reconnaissance and strike drone, a Kasta-2E low-altitude radar, a Nebo-U long-range surveillance radar and two P-18 early warning radars. The unit also struck a drone assembly and repair site and a building housing troops of the 4th Air Assault Battalion of the 108th Air Assault Regiment, although HUR gave no dates or locations for those strikes and did not say whether every target was destroyed or only damaged.

articles.title: Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for Ukraine war talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for talks on Ukraine war
Russia's Vladimir Putin began talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff on ending the Ukraine war in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday, with the American official saying he had brought "ideas" for a possible peace deal.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Norway, where he met Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in talks Washington described as "positive."
The meeting is taking place as the United States pushes an end to Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with Russia pounding Ukrainian cities ahead of winter and amid a bitter feud between Donald Trump and Zelensky.
As Witkoff touched down in Putin's home city, Russia announced it would soon begin shipments of diesel to the United States under a deal with Trump, and that it had freed a US citizen—Stephen Hubbard—held by Moscow since the start of the war on allegations of fighting as a "mercenary" for Ukraine.
"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff—Trump's business partner and envoy—told Putin in Saint Petersburg's Konstantinovsky Palace.
Putin thanked Trump for his efforts to resolve the war and said he was eager to be informed about the US meeting with Zelensky.
The longtime Russian leader has repeatedly refused to hold face-to-face talks with Zelensky and said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Witkoff told Putin he hoped trilateral talks can resume.
"I'm hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process so we can begin to have technical teams discussing what are those next steps," he told the Russian leader.
Putin thanked Trump for his "attention" to the conflict and said the US leader had "insisted that it was necessary to end this conflict" in their last phone call.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of troops on both sides as well as thousands of civilians.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Moscow's strikes killed at least four people —including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
'Momentum' in talks
Meeting Putin, Witkoff described his talks with Zelensky as "productive."
"I think there's some degree of momentum and I hope that today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict," he said.
Zelensky on Tuesday thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting in Norway followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, with Zelensky urging the US not to side with Russia and Trump calling for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is also due to participate in Wednesday's talks with Putin remotely.
US-led talks on the conflict have so far not led to a breakthrough and Moscow insists it intends to press on with its offensive.
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a diesel deal—met with astonishment in Kyiv and across Europe—that saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of testing midterm elections in the US next month.
Washington was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
"We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a "mercenary" fighting for Ukraine.
Witkoff hailed the move and called Putin a "humanitarian".
Trump later said that Hubbard was on his way to the Unites States and that the release had not been part of a swap deal.

articles.title: Trump Envoy Grilled for Calling Putin a ‘Humanitarian’ Amid War in Ukraine
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff sparked outrage among Republican lawmakers Wednesday, Oct. 21, after praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” during talks in St. Petersburg, despite Moscow’s continuing deadly attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
The remarks came as Putin released Stephen Hubbard, an American citizen imprisoned in Russia for more than four years, while Washington sought to revive negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian – you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin during the televised meeting.
“I commend you, and I thank you again,” he added.
The praise drew immediate condemnation from Republican lawmakers, who pointed to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, attacks on civilians and the deportation of Ukrainian children.
‘WTF, Steve?’ – Republicans condemn Witkoff’s praise
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina condemned Witkoff’s praise of Putin as Russian forces continued to bombard Ukrainian cities.
“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis wrote on X.
“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” he added, urging Witkoff to speak with Ukrainian families whose children have been killed or taken to Russia.
Bundeswehr Raises Threat Level, Warns of Potential Russian Attacks
Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas also rejected the envoy’s characterization.
“No. Putin is a stone cold killer,” Cornyn wrote on X.
Republican Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, another outspoken critic of Washington’s approach to Moscow, described the episode as “another embarrassment.”
Trump and Vance defend envoy
Trump played down the controversy when questioned about Witkoff’s remarks, suggesting that the description could be understood in the narrow context of Hubbard’s release.
“Well, I guess you could say (it) for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out,” Trump said.
“But you know, I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other.”
Vice President JD Vance offered a more direct defense, arguing that Witkoff’s comments were part of the diplomacy required to secure an American citizen’s freedom.
“I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage,” Vance said during an event in Ohio.
“Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done.”
The administration has presented Hubbard’s release as a diplomatic success. Trump said Washington had not been required to release another prisoner in exchange.
American teacher released after more than four years in Russian captivity
Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher and US Air Force veteran, had been held by Russia since 2022 after Russian troops detained him in occupied eastern Ukraine.
Russian authorities accused him of fighting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces, allegations his family and legal representatives denied.
He was subsequently sentenced to nearly seven years in prison. The US government designated him as wrongfully detained.
According to the Associated Press, Hubbard’s family described harsh conditions during his detention, including beatings and deprivation of food.
His sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, expressed relief at his release following years of uncertainty over his fate.
The Kremlin presented the decision as a goodwill gesture toward Trump, saying Hubbard had been pardoned following requests from Washington.
Witkoff’s meeting with Putin came one day after discussions with President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners in Oslo.
According to the Ukrainian presidency, the talks focused on security guarantees, possible ceasefire arrangements and proposals to advance negotiations.
Zelensky emphasized the importance of US engagement while making clear that Ukraine was seeking a just and lasting peace rather than an agreement that would leave the country vulnerable to renewed Russian aggression.

articles.title: Zelensky proposes freezing front with Russia as first step to peace talks
articles.body:
Ukraine and Russia both say ready to resume trilateral talks with US
Ukraine and Russia on Wednesday said they are both ready to resume trilateral talks with the United States. The news comes after US envoy Steve Witkoff separately met with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin on two consecutive days.
Russia and Ukraine said Wednesday they were ready to resume trilateral talks with Washington, after US special envoy Steve Witkoff met both countries’ leaders, though the Kremlin decried little “substance” in new Ukrainian and European peace approaches.
Moscow also said a summit between President Vladimir Putin, US counterpart Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping was being prepared in China’s Shenzhen for next month, calling it “the first such meeting in history.”
Putin held over three hours of talks with Witkoff in his home city of Saint Petersburg, a day after what the US official called a “productive” meeting with Ukraine’s Zelensky in Norway.
Witkoff said on social media afterward that the talks were “constructive” but that “there is still important work left to do” and discussions would continue between the US, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level.
As Witkoff touched down in Russia, Moscow freed a US citizen – Stephen Hubbard – and said it would soon begin diesel shipments to America.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the talks with Putin remotely.
Read moreRussia announces release of US citizen Stephen Hubbard during Putin-Witkoff meeting
Over a year of US-led talks to end the Ukraine war – launched by Moscow in 2022 – have not yet led to a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, that Witkoff briefed Putin on “some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv” from the Oslo meeting, adding though that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”.
Putin has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
‘Ideas’ towards a peace deal
Ushakov said a “first-ever” China-US-Russia meeting was “being prepared” in China, without saying what the leaders would discuss.
Kyiv and its European allies have voiced fears that the White House could strike a deal over their heads.
Witkoff held his ninth meeting with Putin as Russia continued to pound Ukrainian cities ahead of winter and amid a bitter feud between Trump and Zelensky.
The US envoy said he wanted trilateral talks to resume, something the Kremlin later said it agreed to.
Zelensky said that Kyiv backed resuming trilateral talks, telling journalists: “We have learned that Russia ... is favourable to a trilateral meeting between our teams. The American side is proposing to organise this meeting as soon as possible. We are in favour of it.”
Ushakov said the talks would re-open in mid-November and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on post-war security.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Russian strikes killed at least four people – including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
Russian occupation authorities in the Lugansk region, meanwhile, said a Ukrainian drone strike on a phone company had killed two people.
‘Momentum’ in talks
Witkoff told Putin he saw “some degree of momentum” in the US-led talks after meeting Zelensky.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting Tuesday followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, and calls from Trump for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was “grateful” for a diesel deal, which saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States, sparking outrage in Kyiv and across Europe.
Read moreTrump strikes diesel deal with Putin, reversing years of pressure on Russia over Ukraine war
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers, as Trump’s Republican Party heads towards tough midterm elections next month.
Washington was interested in further “business and economic cooperation” with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
“We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over,” he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not to lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a “mercenary” fighting for Ukraine.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
