articles.title: Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
articles.body:
Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
Russia is ready to resume three-way negotiations with the US and Ukraine to discuss security arrangements for when the conflict has ended, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
The announcement followed nearly three hours of talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Jared Kushner joined by video link after illness prevented him from traveling.
Ushakov said Putin told Witkoff that Moscow was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations in mid-November, with the main topic being a post-conflict security system for Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff indicated that Trump would welcome the proposal, the aide added.
The presidential aide noted that earlier attempts to restart trilateral talks were derailed by Kiev having carried out massive attacks on Moscow and other cities during Russia’s recent parliamentary elections. Polling stations were targeted on the main voting day, with election commission personnel killed.
However, the situation has since been “re-evaluated, taking into account the signals received from the Americans,” Ushakov said, adding that Putin had praised the mediation efforts of Trump, his administration, and special representatives in seeking mutually acceptable solutions.
The Russian president also presented an “objective picture of the situation along the line of contact, where Russian troops hold complete strategic initiative,” and noted that Moscow’s forces are conducting a “relentless offensive in all key areas” and effectively destroying military-industrial, energy, and logistics facilities in Ukraine.
Beyond Ukraine, the participants discussed the October diesel agreement, under which Washington eased sanctions on Russian fuel exports. Both sides said the deal served their interests and would help stabilize global fuel markets. Other joint economic projects are also approaching implementation, Ushakov added.
Russia, Ukraine and the US last held talks in Geneva in February, following two rounds in Abu Dhabi. Further negotiations, however, were put on hold after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, disrupting access to the UAE.
Ushakov told Russian media that Abu Dhabi was again being examined as a possible venue for renewed talks, noting that Putin has yet to choose the members of a future Russian delegation.
Asked by reporters whether the Ukraine conflict was approaching its end, Ushakov suggested it is “moving in that direction.”

articles.title: China and Russia push Japan’s jet scrambles to 4-year high
articles.body:
- Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighters 442 times from April to September 2026, up from 265 in the same period of 2025.
- Scrambles against Russian aircraft rose from 59 to 152, while those against Chinese aircraft and drones climbed from 198 to 285.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets 442 times between April 1 and Sept. 30, about two-thirds more than the 265 scrambles in the same period last year, according to Joint Staff Office figures reported by USNI News. The rise came as Chinese and Russian military aircraft flew near Japan far more often, and the six-month total for the first half of Japan’s 2026 fiscal year is the highest first-half count since fiscal 2022, when JASDF fighters launched 446 times.
None of the flights crossed into Japanese sovereign airspace, and the report lists no airspace violations during the period. Japan scrambles fighters against foreign aircraft approaching the country and entering its Air Defense Identification Zone, a monitoring area that reaches well past the 12-nautical-mile (22 km) territorial limit into international airspace.
Chinese aircraft and drones accounted for 285 scrambles, or about 65 percent, up from 198 a year earlier. The sharper change came from Russia, as JASDF fighters launched 152 times against Russian aircraft compared with 59 in the first half of fiscal 2025, which is more than in the first half of any of the four previous fiscal years listed in the report. The remaining five scrambles were classed as “other.”
The Joint Staff Office pointed to three patterns behind the numbers: Russian Il-20 intelligence-gathering flights over the Sea of Japan and the Pacific, Chinese Y-9 intelligence flights over the East China Sea, and long-range joint flights by Chinese H-6 and Russian Tu-95 bombers. Japan reported Y-9 flights on five consecutive days from Sept. 3 to Sept. 7, after we reported on an Aug. 12 Y-9 sortie through the same corridor between the Danjo Islands and Okinawa.
The southwest, which faces Taiwan and the East China Sea, remained the busiest sector, with the Southwestern Air Defense Force logging 201 scrambles against 189 a year earlier. The Northern Air Defense Force, which covers Hokkaido and northern Honshu opposite Russia’s Sakhalin Island, more than doubled its count from 53 to 112. The Central Air Defense Force rose from nine to 27.
The steepest jump came in the Western Air Defense Force, which covers Kyushu, Shikoku and western Honshu and went from 14 scrambles to 102. USNI News, citing the Joint Staff flight-path map, attributed the increase to Chinese activity over the East China Sea and to Russian aircraft flying from the Sea of Japan to the East China Sea to link up with Chinese formations.
The largest single event came on June 27, when two H-6 bombers and two J-16 fighters flew from the East China Sea into the Sea of Japan. There they joined two Russian Tu-95 bombers, two Tu-142 maritime patrol aircraft and a Su-35 fighter. The combined group flew back to the East China Sea, where the Russian bombers and patrol aircraft met another two H-6s and four J-16s, passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island and continued on a long-range flight over the Pacific south of Shikoku.
South Korea also scrambled fighters that day after nearly 10 Chinese and Russian aircraft entered and left its own air defense zone, and Seoul lodged a protest with both countries the next day. It was the first joint bomber flight around Japan since a December 2025 mission that paired two Tu-95s with two H-6s and eight J-16s. Beijing and Moscow describe such patrols as normal cooperation, while Japan’s 2026 defense white paper says repeated joint activities are “obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan.”
The report also lists 25 publicly announced cases of unusual flight activity during the six months. Chinese Y-9 flights account for 13 of them, twice accompanied by a TB-001 reconnaissance and strike drone, while Russian Il-20 flights appear 10 times. The only other bomber entry covers July 21, when a single Tu-95 and a Su-35 flew over the Sea of Japan.
The surge follows a quieter year. Japan recorded 595 scrambles in all of fiscal 2025, including 214 against Russian aircraft, and monthly counts climbed late in that year, reaching 79 in December 2025. That same month, Japan accused J-15 fighters from the carrier Liaoning of directing their radar at two JASDF F-15s southeast of Okinawa.
The pace held through the summer, with 90 scrambles in July and 76 in August, as Chinese intelligence aircraft and drones and Russian intelligence planes kept up flights around Japan.

articles.title: Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
articles.body:
Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
BERLIN, Oct 21 - Germany's armed forces classified the threat of Russian sabotage against their own troops and facilities as "significant" for the first time, the second-highest level on their internal threat scale, according to a Bundeswehr assessment reported by German broadcasters WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung on Wednesday.
A defence ministry spokesperson confirmed the assessment, telling reporters: "We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for the Bundeswehr."
The reassessment was triggered by the discovery in mid-September of a crashed drone carrying a tin of high explosives near the Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.
CROSSED 'RED LINE'
The internal document, seen by WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said Russia had crossed "a previously anticipated red line of harmful intent involving kinetic and/or lethal effects" against Germany and the Bundeswehr through the use of weaponised drones.
The Wunstorf drone resembles one laden with explosives that was used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. But unlike the Leipzig incident, which authorities said targeted civilian cargo aircraft, investigators believe the Wunstorf drone was aimed at Bundeswehr aircraft, the document is cited as saying.
Germany has blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack.
Moscow denied involvement and has consistently rejected accusations of carrying out sabotage or hybrid attacks in Europe.
The report also cited a pattern of suspected Russian reconnaissance across Germany, including drone overflights of the Arrow 3 missile defence site in Saxony-Anhalt, and a camouflaged camera found filming a strategically important railway station in Minden, Westphalia.
Intelligence services expect the situation to worsen in the short term, with further actions likely in the near future, the document says, according to WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
The defence ministry spokesperson said preventive measures were being tailored to individual sites and could range from increased guard patrols to additional technical security such as infrared cameras and fence surveillance systems.
The assessment comes just over a week after German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany faced a "shadow war" and called for expanded intelligence powers.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that Russian disinformation and hybrid attacks posed the biggest threat to Germany. "My view is that our people are still underestimating this big threat to our society... This is a fundamental attack against the entire political order we achieved after 1990." REUTERS

articles.title: UAE-made armored vehicles seen again in Russia
articles.body:
- Russia’s Gyurza SOBR unit in the Moscow region has been seen with a Cobra-LAMV armored vehicle made by Emirati company Streit Group.
- Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have sanctioned Streit Group over vehicles supplied to Russia’s National Guard.
Armored vehicles built by Emirati manufacturer Streit Group have been spotted again in Russian service, this time with Gyurza, the special rapid response unit (SOBR) of Rosgvardia’s Main Directorate for the Moscow region, which was photographed operating a Cobra-LAMV 4×4. The light armored vehicle is built on a Toyota Land Cruiser chassis and marketed by Streit to police and internal security forces. It continues to turn up with Russia’s National Guard even though Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have all sanctioned the company over its vehicles reaching Russia.
Cobra vehicles first appeared in Russia in October 2024, when a Russian military blogger published video of a shipment of more than 20 Streit-built Spartan, Cobra and Cougar armored vehicles bound for Russian forces, as we were first to report. In September 2025, Rosgvardia units were filmed training with Spartan SUT vehicles, including one fitted with an 82 mm (3.2-inch) mortar in the rear compartment, we reported at the time. Every one of these deliveries reached Russia well after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine was the first to respond, listing Streit Group in 2023, and the European Union and Switzerland followed in October 2025 before adding founder Guerman Goutorov personally to their sanctions lists in May 2026. Canada sanctioned the company in August 2026 for supplying vehicles to Rosgvardia, a move Russia’s ambassador in Ottawa dismissed as having no practical effect, and the new Moscow-region sighting shows that the vehicles keep reaching Russian units regardless.
The Canadian measures carry particular weight because Streit started out as a Canadian business founded in Ontario in 1992 by Goutorov, a Russian-born businessman who served five years in the Soviet police before emigrating to Canada in the early 1990s. He later moved the company’s headquarters to the Ras Al Khaimah free trade zone in the United Arab Emirates, where Streit grew into one of the world’s largest armored vehicle makers with production sites on several continents. Goutorov’s Canadian citizenship shields him personally from Ottawa’s sanctions, and he has appealed his listing in the European Union.
Streit’s links to Russia go well beyond finished vehicles, since the company opened an armored vehicle plant east of Moscow and another in Tatarstan in 2009 and kept trading with Russian suppliers after both the 2014 and 2022 invasions. Customs records show that between 2015 and 2022 it imported 41 shipments of parts from Russian truckmaker Kamaz and 38 shipments of VPK-Ural vehicle kits, including six from the sanctioned Arzamas plant in the two weeks before Russian troops crossed into Ukraine. The company also worked with Russia’s Military-Industrial Company on armored vehicles that were later used by Wagner Group fighters in several conflict zones.
Russia is far from the only controversial destination for Streit vehicles, which have repeatedly surfaced in conflict zones under arms embargoes or in the hands of armed groups. In Yemen, Houthi military media released footage of armored vehicles captured from Saudi-backed forces. In Iran, a Toophan MRAP displayed at the Eghtedar 40 military exhibition in Tehran in 2019 was photographed and described as the same design as Streit’s Typhoon, although Iranian sources present the vehicle as a domestic development.
UN expert panels have accused Streit of breaking arms embargoes on Libya and Sudan and criticized the sale of hundreds of its vehicles into South Sudan, as we reported in 2016. Its vehicles have since been delivered to Khalifa Haftar’s forces in eastern Libya and seen with riot police in Belarus and with Guinea’s military junta. In 2015, Streit’s U.S. subsidiary paid a $3.5 million fine and Goutorov personally paid $250,000 over unlicensed exports of armored vehicles to Afghanistan, Iraq, Nigeria and other countries.
Streit has denied wrongdoing every time its vehicles have surfaced in such places, insisting that it follows UAE export law, ships its vehicles without weapons and bears no responsibility for how buyers modify or use them after sale. The company has never explained how its armored vehicles continue to reach Rosgvardia units more than four years into Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Putin ‘Ready’ for Three-Way Ukraine Talks in November, Kremlin Says
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff that Moscow was ready in principle to resume three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the US around mid-November, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
Ushakov said Putin conveyed that position during their meeting in St. Petersburg. The proposed discussions would focus on postwar security arrangements.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations,” Ushakov told journalists, according to Interfax Russia.
The aide added that Moscow’s main proposed topic was establishing a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the fighting ends.
Ushakov also said Witkoff indicated that US President Donald Trump would welcome Russia’s willingness to return to negotiations. The Kremlin aide provided that description of the envoy’s response.
The announcement set out Moscow’s position and a proposed timeframe, rather than a jointly announced agreement among the three countries on when negotiations would take place.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said it is open to direct talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky, but it has demanded that the Ukrainian leader come to Moscow, effectively derailing the proposals.
Witkoff brings proposals from Oslo
The Kremlin’s statement followed Witkoff’s arrival in St. Petersburg with proposals discussed with Ukrainian and European leaders.
Russian Su-30 Crashes Near NATO Borders, Pilots Eject
During Wednesday’s meeting, the US envoy said he had brought documents outlining possible approaches to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. He urged Putin to consider restarting negotiations involving representatives of all three countries, including technical working groups.
Witkoff described the preceding discussions in Oslo as productive and said they could move toward a ceasefire. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin would review the proposals.
The visit marked the US envoys’ first trip to Russia since Sept. 5, when Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Putin and senior Russian officials for three hours before traveling to Kyiv.
Before Wednesday’s meeting, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow would listen to US proposals but ruled out political concessions.
Ukraine seeks strong security guarantees
Security guarantees were also central to Zelensky’s talks with Witkoff and Nordic leaders in Norway on Tuesday, Oct. 20.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Witkoff would take proposals developed during the Oslo discussions to Russia’s leadership. The talks covered Ukraine’s security, territorial questions, sanctions and postwar prosperity.
Zelensky said a draft document included several types of guarantees, which Kyiv would present to the Russian side before assessing Putin’s response.
The Ukrainian president also confirmed that US intelligence sharing for early warnings of Russian attacks had resumed after a week of interruptions.
He said he expected progress within 48 hours on Patriot interceptors, intelligence cooperation and restrictions affecting Starlink terminals. Those issues formed part of the broader discussions over Ukraine’s ability to defend itself while diplomacy continued.
Kyiv rejects Ukraine peace talks without Ukraine
The proposed Russia-US-Ukraine format comes as Zelensky has rejected any attempt to negotiate Ukraine’s future without Kyiv.
Speaking in Oslo, he responded to reports of a possible separate meeting involving Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelensky said those leaders could hold their own discussions, but any negotiations on Ukraine’s future require Ukrainian participation.
He distinguished that potential summit from the three-way meeting he had proposed involving the US, Ukraine and Russia.
The Ukrainian president said the security proposals discussed in Oslo included arrangements resembling NATO’s Article 5 collective defense commitment. He emphasized that Ukraine needed strong guarantees after the war ends, and Kyiv was awaiting feedback from Witkoff’s discussions in Russia.
Støre likewise reaffirmed that decisions about Ukraine’s future could not be made without Ukraine’s involvement.

articles.title: Quantum Systems Gets Interceptor Drone Up to 777 km/h
articles.body:
German company Quantum Systems has developed the Apex Recordhunter technology demonstrator, which reached a speed of 777 km/h.
Quantum Systems representatives told Militarnyi details about the project and shared a post on social media.
The company’s N3XT research and development division is responsible for developing the aircraft.
The need for such systems arose from Russia’s use of jet-powered strike drones capable of reaching speeds of 600 km/h, creating demand for faster interceptors.
“Russia is using jet-powered strike drones, such as the Geran-5, with speeds of up to 600 km/h. This creates a need for faster interceptors capable of keeping pace with the evolving threat,” Quantum Systems said.
To achieve high speeds, the developers combined a revised aerodynamic design, a powerful electric motor and a cooling system in a compact airframe.
The drone accelerated from 0 to 777 km/h in 27 seconds.
It reached this speed for a fraction of a second, after which the pilot began slowing down and landed the aircraft.
During the flight, the engineers’ main challenge was ensuring the aircraft’s stability, as even minor deviations create additional drag and consume energy.
The project’s findings are already being applied to the development of new counter-UAV systems.
Militarnyi previously reported that Germany will fund the production in Ukraine of tens of thousands of Quantum Systems interceptor drones to strengthen defenses against Russian strike UAVs.
The funding will be part of Germany’s military aid package for Ukraine for the winter of 2026-2027.

articles.title: Why Rubio is seeking India’s help after coercion over Russian oil
articles.body:
Why Rubio is seeking India’s help after coercion over Russian oil
After spending years pressuring New Delhi to cut back its Russian oil purchases, and isolate Moscow, Washington has now changed tack and is seeking India’s help to bring down elevated domestic fuel prices that are largely of its own making.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who skipped New Delhi entirely on his second visit to India this year, made clear what had brought him to the country – the massive refining capacity of Reliance Industries, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani.
“I’m also here in my capacity as the National Security Adviser,” Rubio said in Mumbai. “Energy is related to national security … we’re going to go see a company that has a tremendous amount of refining capability.”
President Donald Trump’s administration is showing a new urgency to bring down the high fuel prices that threaten Republicans’ prospects in November’s midterm elections. US retail diesel prices reached a record average of about $6.32 a gallon on Tuesday.
American refineries are already operating at close to capacity, and Washington is working with India to increase refining output and bring more petroleum products to global markets, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in Houston the same day.
“Energy politics is inseparable from American geopolitics,” Jindal School of International Affairs adjunct professor and former Jawaharlal Nehru University professor Anuradha Mitra Chenoy told RT. “The US is using energy as a geopolitical instrument, and that is central to understanding Rubio’s visit.”
From Russian oil tariffs to Venezuelan crude
Washington has regularly used energy sanctions to achieve its geopolitical aims. First it took Iranian, and then Venezuelan, crude off the market with the threat of sanctions. Since the Ukraine conflict began, Washington also pressured India to stop buying Russian crude. The argument was that choking off Moscow’s oil revenues would help end the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.
At the same time, the US continued to supply Ukraine with weapons and funds, and started a war with Iran that disrupted energy supplies from the Middle East.
New Delhi has maintained that providing affordable energy to its 1.4 billion people is central to its oil-purchasing decisions. India imports about 85% of its energy requirements, and Russia remains one of its biggest sources of oil.
But the pressure reached a breaking point when the US Congress passed a law last month that threatened “bone-crushing sanctions” on major buyers of Russian energy. New Delhi warned that the proposed measures could affect bilateral relations and global energy markets.
However, as the affordability crisis in America got worse, and Trump’s rhetoric failed to bring down domestic fuel prices in a connected global market, the administration swiftly changed course.
Trump announced a deal with Russia to buy diesel for the domestic market. And cleared the deck for Rubio’s visit by waiving off sanctions on Moscow’s top oil buyers – which includes China and India, allowing Russian oil to flow more freely into global markets.
“None of these tariffs are meant to punish or harm India,” Rubio said in Mumbai, adopting a more conciliatory tone than has come out of Washington until recently.
Why Reliance, and Jamnagar, matter to Washington
Washington’s top diplomat held talks with Mukesh Ambani at Jamnagar in India’s Gujarat state on the second day of his visit. The Reliance refinery in Jamnagar is the largest single-site refining complex in the world, and can process around 1.4 million barrels of crude a day.
It is also one of the few facilities capable of processing large volumes of Venezuela’s extra-heavy crude, which is good for producing diesel – showing its importance to a US administration worried about domestic fuel prices.
Jamnagar already plays a major part in keeping global fuel prices in check – by selling fuel refined from Russian crude to markets including Europe, which sanctions the same crude.
And it is buying more Venezuelan oil, accounting for more than 74% of the nearly $3.6 billion worth of Venezuelan crude imported by India between April and August, according to figures shared by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) think tank.
Rubio wants Reliance to buy, and process, more of the Venezuelan crude, which the US now controls after kidnapping the country’s President Nicolas Maduro.
“The refining capability exists,” GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava told RT. “The question is whether expanding purchases makes commercial sense.”
Venezuelan crude is cheaper but it also costs more to refine, he pointed out. He also questioned the wisdom of India buying more of the South American country’s oil, which was once subjected to US sanctions.
“It would be very unwise for India to stop using Russian oil,” Chenoy said, pointing out that there are only a limited number of major sources available internationally, and Russia remains one of the most important.
Reliance is also involved in a proposed refinery project in Brownsville, Texas, under a long-term agreement to purchase its output. The facility, which Trump called a $300 billion project in March, is designed to process lighter American shale crude.
The Indian conglomerate “helps utilize and unleash the energy that is being developed in the Western Hemisphere,” Rubio told the Indian Express, describing his visit as an opportunity to identify ways of diversifying energy supplies.
Rubio dodges a Musk-ignited controversy
Ahead of his meeting with Ambani, Rubio had to sidestep the controversy ignited by trillionaire Elon Musk.
The world’s richest man, a prominent donor to the Republican party, had accused Ambani earlier this month of obstructing the launch of his Starlink satellite internet service in India.
Musk targeted Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and questioning whether his company would allow Starlink to compete in the country.
Starlink, Ambani’s Jio Satellite Communications, and Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are all at broadly the same stage of regulatory approval for satellite internet connectivity in the country, with security assessments underway, according to India’s Communications Ministry.
Reliance also dismissed suggestions that it was blocking competition.
“Elon Musk is a private citizen,” Rubio told the Indian Express, adding that Musk had the right to express his views.
Rubio also sought to assuage concerns about the India-US trade deal, which has been holding fire despite months of tortuous negotiations. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the talks as deadlocked earlier this month, saying both sides were finding it “very difficult” to make further concessions.
“We are weeks, not months, away from, I think, finalizing it,” Rubio said. “I would say we are about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement.”
India has been holding off on finalizing the deal as it wants to lock in a competitive advantage in the US market relative to rival exporter nations.
Pragmatism back on the table
The US administration turning on the charm, so to speak, suggests that Washington’s energy and political interests are taking precedence over its geopolitical considerations and moral grandstanding.
With pragmatism back on the table, Rubio’s visit could mark a step toward easing bilateral tensions and strengthening cooperation beyond the immediate fuel crisis driving the change.
Still India must “carefully examine what it is being asked to commit to, what commercial benefits it can expect, and the risks of future changes in US policy,” Srivastava said.

articles.title: The Kremlin warned Germany of new acts of sabotage after an attempt to blow up a Ukrainian aircraft in Leipzig – WSJ
articles.body:
The Kremlin warned Germany of new acts of sabotage after an attempt to blow up a Ukrainian aircraft in Leipzig – WSJ
Kyiv • UNN
WSJ: A Russian official said that Leipzig will not be the last target. U.S. intelligence believes that Putin ordered an intensification of attacks against NATO.
A Kremlin representative, following the exposure of an attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig Airport, warned the German government that Russia does not intend to stop attacks on European territory. According to U.S. intelligence, the order to intensify the sabotage campaign against NATO countries was personally issued by Vladimir Putin. The Wall Street Journal reports this, citing sources, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, after the incident in Leipzig, a Russian official contacted a representative of the German government and warned that this airport would not be Moscow’s last target. The journalists did not disclose the official’s name.
In August 2026, German law enforcement officers discovered a drone carrying explosives near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft at Leipzig Airport. It later emerged that there had been several drones. On September 1, Berlin officially accused Russia of preparing an act of sabotage, but Moscow rejected the accusations.
Putin personally ordered the intensification of sabotage against NATO
As reported by the WSJ, U.S. intelligence established that dissatisfaction grew in the Kremlin over the summer due to the lack of results both on the battlefield and in negotiations with the United States. Ukraine did not agree to Putin’s demands despite military and diplomatic pressure.
According to sources familiar with the findings of U.S. intelligence agencies, it was Putin who ordered the intensification of sabotage and covert operations against NATO states. CIA Director John Ratcliffe personally warned European intelligence services and politicians about preparations for a new wave of Russian operations after his trip to Moscow.
Following the incident in Leipzig, European countries recorded a number of suspicious attacks. In particular, in August, arson attacks took place at drone-manufacturing facilities in Estonia and Poland. Slovak law enforcement officials also reported that they had prevented an arson attack at a plant producing Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: Russia ready for 3-way talks on Ukraine war, Kremlin says
articles.body:
Russian leader Vladimir Putin is “in principle” ready for Moscow to resume talks with Washington and Kyiv, the Kremlin said Wednesday.
During a meeting in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, Putin said Moscow is ready to restart trilateral negotiations in November, Yuri Ushakov, a senior Putin aide, told reporters.
Ushakov added that the “conflict in Ukraine is coming to an end,” and said trilateral talks “may take place in Abu Dhabi.”
Advertisement
Witkoff confirmed on X that discussions “will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level.”
His visit was the latest in a new round of U.S. attempts to bring Moscow to the negotiating table to end its war against Ukraine. The special envoy also met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, subsequently announcing a proposal for a three-way leaders’ negotiation.
There have been several rounds of talks between the U.S. and Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The most recent discussions stalled in February when the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran.
Previous negotiations were largely political theater and failed to yield any broader breakthrough on halting hostilities, prisoner-of-war exchanges or a truce regarding strikes on energy infrastructure.
Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported Moscow proposed a potential high-level summit with China and the U.S. to negotiate a deal on ending the war in Ukraine.
On Wednesday, footage emerged of Witkoff praising Putin during their face-to-face talks in St. Petersburg, after the Russians released a U.S. prisoner from captivity.

Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" during talks in St. Petersburg - media

U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff called Putin a humanitarian during a meeting in St. Petersburg. He is trying to organize talks between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia.
United States Special Envoy Steve Witkoff assessed kremlin chief vladimir putin during personal talks in st. petersburg, calling him a "humanitarian." Politico reports, writes UNN.

Witkoff's visit is the latest attempt by the United States to bring moscow and Kyiv to the negotiating table four and a half years after the kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the outlet notes.
The American envoy met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday and was expected to propose trilateral talks between the two leaders and U.S. President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles – a series of explosions rang out in the capital
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles – a series of explosions rang out in the capital 21 October 2026
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 22, Kyiv was attacked by ballistic missiles; at least four explosions were recorded. There was no information about casualties or damage.
During the night of October 22, Russian forces launched a missile strike on Kyiv. At least four powerful explosions were heard in the capital, while the Ukrainian Air Force warned of ballistic missiles approaching from the east, UNN reports.
Details
At 1:55 a.m., the Air Force announced a threat of ballistic weapons being used from the north. Already at 1:57 a.m., the military reported missiles over Poltava region moving westward and уточнили, що їхньою ціллю є Київ.
At 1:59 a.m., the Air Force detected ballistic missiles moving from the east toward Boryspil and the capital. Shortly afterward, a series of explosions rang out in Kyiv.
What is known about the missile attack
According to monitoring channels, Russia may have used Zircon missiles, which were allegedly launched from Rostov region. At the same time, the Air Force had not officially confirmed the type of missiles or the location from which they were launched.
At around 2:01 a.m., monitoring resources reported that the current wave of the missile attack had ended, but warned that the threat of new launches remained.
No information about possible destruction or casualties had been received at the time of the first reports.

articles.title: Russia Builds 33 Air Defense Positions Around Alabuga Drone Production Zone
articles.body:
A total of 33 air defense positions have been established around Russia’s Alabuga special economic zone, where Shahed/Geran-type drones are manufactured.
Satellite images showing the new positions were published by Radio Liberty.
Satellite imagery dated October 21 shows that, since spring 2026, concrete towers for air defense systems and new sites for surface-to-air missile systems have been built in the area.
Towers equipped with anti-aircraft machine guns and structures for stretching anti-drone nets over production buildings have also been installed.
Ukrainian drones last reached Alabuga in 2025.
In September, satellite imagery showed the emergence of new production workshops and warehouses within the Alabuga special economic zone.
The infrastructure is being expanded amid the recruitment of foreign workers to manufacture strike drones for Russia.
Russia has also increased production of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered strike drones to 4,000 per month, twice the output of piston-powered Geran-2 drones.

articles.title: Her own city is under Russian fire, yet Kyiv woman urges killing Ukrainians among nearly 100,000 pro-Kremlin posts in two years. She faces up to 12 years
articles.body:
Russia bombs Kyiv almost every day. Inside the same city, a single account spent two years pumping out nearly 100,000 posts in Russia’s favor. Ukraine’s Security Service has served notices of suspicion on six more pro-Kremlin agitators across the country, among them the Kyiv woman behind those posts, which included calls to kill Ukrainians, the agency said.
Social media has become a channel for spreading hatred during the war, and the scale is striking. Except for Russian narratives, the Kyiv suspect also incited violence against a national minority and called for destroying the churches of religious communities, the agency said.
The agency framed the six as part of a wider effort to justify Russia’s aggression and inflame ethnic and religious hatred. Investigators notified them of suspicion.
Six accounts, one message from the Kremlin
The others span the country. In Mykolaiv, SBU cyber specialists detained a person they say acted on a Russian handler’s orders, administering a local Telegram channel of more than 13,000 subscribers in support of Russian forces, investigators said.
In Cherkasy Oblast, the wife of a priest of the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church allegedly praised Vladimir Putin and denied Russia’s aggression in Telegram chats, while a Russian citizen with permanent residence in Ukraine allegedly called the full-scale war an “internal civil conflict.” In Zakarpattia region, two women allegedly urged the region’s “separation” from Ukraine.
What the suspects face, and where this fits
The charges are grave. The suspects were notified under several articles of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, including inciting ethnic and religious hatred combined with threats and justifying Russian aggression, and face up to 12 years in prison with confiscation of property, the agency said.
The sweep continues a long campaign against homegrown pro-Russian propagandists. In February, the SBU detained three suspected agitators who used Telegram and TikTok to call for missile strikes on Kyiv and to justify Russian war crimes, part of a pattern in which Moscow recruits users online to spread its narratives.

articles.title: Starlink slowdown makes Ukraine’s Shahed-hunting drone maker rethink air-launched interceptors
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone maker Wild Hornets is rethinking projects it is currently working on, including launching interceptors from aerial platforms, because of limits on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet. Spokesman Mike Orliuk told The War Zone (TWZ) this on 20 October. The company builds Sting interceptors, which it says destroyed over 15,000 Shaheds and Gerberas, a cheaper Shahed lookalike, in a year. Orliuk said Sting’s current operations are unaffected.
The stakes rise as Russia shifts to faster drones. Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov counted more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans, Russia’s version of the Shahed, in August. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 16 October that these drones fly faster than 400 km/h. He added that some Ukrainian interceptors chasing them work through Starlink. When the link was slowed, Ukraine could not intercept some of them, he said.
How Sting stays connected
“Our own communications system provides the basic connection to our interceptors,” Orliuk said. The company’s remote-control technology can draw on various internet sources, he added, though the military often uses Starlink. Even then, the terminal does not need to move at high speed. It only links the command center to a ground station, which Orliuk compared to a cell tower.
“For these needs, everything is operating normally with Starlink at the moment,” he said.
An air-launch project under review
“Some drones carry a terminal on board and need to fly at high speed with it,” Orliuk said. “In such cases, Starlink’s limitations make their operation impossible.”
That is why the company is rethinking the air-launch project. Wild Hornets has made no clear decision yet but will test alternatives, Orliuk said. He declined to describe them.
“I believe, in any case, depending on a single solution is very risky,” he said.
Musk pointed at the US military over Ukraine’s satellite limits. Now a US official says the administration had nothing to do with them
Other firms share the concern
Orliuk said he has spoken with other companies that rely far more on Starlink and have expressed concerns. He pointed to growing interest in Europe’s Eutelsat network, though “creating something like Starlink won’t be easy.”
Who ordered the slowdown remains unclear. The order to slow Ukraine’s Starshield service came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official said. A US official told TWZ the president never made such a request. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on 17 October that the slowdown had “nothing to do with the White House” and called “a report on that” “categorically false,” without saying which report he meant.

articles.title: Nuclear safety risk grows: Russian-occupied nuclear plant’s cooling pond keeps sinking, Russia runs short of diesel and staff, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant is short of cooling water, diesel, and qualified staff, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) said on 20 October, warning of rising risks to nuclear safety. The water level in the plant’s cooling pond fell to 12.27 meters on 12 October, down from 12.86 meters in July, while the plant needs at least 15 meters to fully meet its needs, according to HUR. Russian managers are also considering cutting the number of backup generators kept on automatic standby, which would inevitably raise the risk of emergencies, the intelligence agency said.
Europe’s largest nuclear plant has been under Russian control since March 2022. Its six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, but they and their spent fuel still need constant cooling, which depends on water, on a single remaining external power line, and on diesel generators as the last resort. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) warned on 16 October that depleted diesel reserves increase the risk that nuclear safety is challenged if the plant loses power again, and that the situation may become acute in winter.
A pond with no source to refill it
The cooling pond has been sinking since Russia destroyed the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, cutting off the reservoir that fed it. Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear operator, recorded 15.70 meters in October 2023. By June 2025, the level had fallen below 14 meters against a norm of above 16, Oleh Korikov, head of Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate, said.
HUR’s figures show the decline continuing this year, from 12.86 meters in July to 12.63 in early August, 12.55 at the end of August, and 12.34 at the start of October. In 2025, the IAEA said groundwater wells on site were supplying cooling water for the safety systems. Its team had not been allowed to inspect a new dam in the cooling channel, access IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi called essential to assess the cooling water situation.
Diesel for a blackout that Russia cannot supply
If the plant loses external power, its diesel generators would burn about 150 metric tons of fuel a day in a prolonged blackout, HUR said. The occupation administration cannot deliver enough, so reserves stay minimal. Russian managers are also looking for covert fuel supplies, including low-quality fuel, without informing the IAEA mission, according to HUR.
The IAEA has already reported fewer generators on automatic standby. Since late September, only four of the plant’s 20 emergency generators would start automatically in a blackout, with the rest needing manual connection, which Grossi said deviates from normal practice. No diesel deliveries have reached the plant since March, the agency said on 16 October.
The plant spent nearly three weeks on generators after losing its last external line on 20 August, EP reported, until the Ferosplavna-1 line was restored under an IAEA-brokered ceasefire. The main 750 kV Dniprovska line remains out. HUR said the Kremlin rejected Ukraine’s proposal to supply power through it, which raises the nuclear safety risks.
Russia blacked out Europe’s largest nuclear plant 15 times since occupying it in 2022
A plant short of the people who know it
About 5,000 people now work at the plant, against roughly 11,000 before the full-scale invasion, and only 1,450 were on site, HUR said. The plant lacks specialists who know its equipment, as well as the experts needed for repairs and for reconnecting it to external power. Russian managers plan training courses for applicants from Russian regions to replace Ukrainian staff, according to HUR.
In Enerhodar, the city where the plant’s staff live, mobile, internet, electricity, and water supplies keep failing, HUR said.

articles.title: Ukraine's General Staff: 269 combat clashes on battlefield in 24 hours, Russians launched 37 attacks on Kostiantynivka front
articles.body:
Ukraine's General Staff: 269 combat clashes on battlefield in 24 hours, Russians launched 37 attacks on Kostiantynivka front
A total of 269 combat clashes have occurred on the battlefield over the past day, with the Russians conducting 37 attacks on the Kostiantynivka front, 30 on the Pokrovsk front and 20 on the Huliaipole front.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 21 October
Details: A total of 269 combat clashes were recorded over the past day.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, the Russians conducted three airstrikes, using six guided bombs, and conducted 53 strikes on Ukrainian military positions and settlements.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian units repelled 13 Russian attacks. The Russians attacked near the settlements of Ternova, Izbytske, Starytsia, Blahodatne, Symynivka, Vovchanski Khutory, Zakharivka, Okhrimivka, Volokhivske, Vilkhuvatka and Chuhunivka.
On the Kupiansk front, the Russians made eight attempts to improve their positions, conducting offensive operations towards the settlements of Radkivka and Mala Shapkivka.
On the Lyman front, Ukrainian forces repelled Russian attempts to break through their defences. The Russians conducted three assaults, including towards the village of Zarichne.
On the Sloviansk front, the Russians conducted nine attacks near the settlements of Ozerne, Kryva Luka, Orikhuvatka and Yurkivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russians did not conduct any assaults.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 37 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted offensive operations near the city of Kostiantynivka and towards Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia, Novopavlivka, Hruzke, Pryiut, Dobropillia, Vilne, Kolodiazi and Kucheriv Yar.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 30 attacks. They attempted to advance towards the settlements of Dobropillia, Hannivka, Dorozhnie, Novyi Donbas, Krasnopodillia, Bilytske, Serhiivka, Myrne, Molodetske, Novopavlivka and Muravka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the Russians conducted one assault towards the village of Myrne.
On the Huliaipole front, the Russians conducted 20 attacks on Ukrainian positions. They attempted to advance towards the settlements of Rybne, Nove Zaporizhzhia, Rivne, Kosivtseve, Ternuvate, Verkhnia Tersa, Hirke, Zaliznychne, Omelnyk, Novoselivka and Yehorivka.
On the Orikhiv front, the Russians made two attempts to attack towards the settlements of Novoiakivka and Novoandriivka.
On the Prydniprovske front, the Russians did not conduct any assaults.
On the Volyn and Polissia fronts, there is no evidence of any offensive Russian groups being formed in the area.

articles.title: Musk Capped Ukraine’s Starlink Speeds, According to Report
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered a speed restriction on a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service used by Ukraine, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials.
Ukraine depends on Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations, meaning restrictions on the service affect both its offensive and defensive missions against Russia.
Musk imposed a speed cap last week on Ukrainian hardware connecting to the satellite network, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed sources. The measure left some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless, according to the report.
Two people told the Wall Street Journal that Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the decision during a phone call shortly after the slowdown became public.
According to the newspaper, some US officials believed Musk had acted independently and that Trump had not explicitly ordered retaliation against Ukraine. However, a person familiar with the matter said Musk had spoken with several senior administration officials, including Trump, before introducing the speed restriction.
Musk and Trump have both voiced anger over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks. Trump has blamed the strikes for driving up energy prices.
The report follows Trump’s remarks last week that he did not believe either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing access to Starlink.
Musk had previously said that decisions to restrict the service’s speed or use were made by the US military or the president.
Musk, SpaceX, and the White House have not yet responded to the newspaper’s report.
Meanwhile, US envoy Steve Witkoff is scheduled to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday, following what a US official described as “constructive” talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway, as Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war.

articles.title: Russia wants AI to help design its next aircraft
articles.body:
- Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said it is evaluating new software, including artificial intelligence, to speed up the design of future aircraft and modifications.
- UAC is already running a pilot project with Sberbank’s GigaChat AI for generative design at the early stage of a new aircraft.
Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation is looking at artificial intelligence and other new software to speed up the design of future aircraft and cut the cost of developing new versions of existing ones, the state-owned planemaker said in a statement on its social media.
UAC, which builds nearly all of Russia’s military and civil aircraft, from Su-57 and Su-35 fighters to the MC-21 airliner, said its engineers are evaluating new software products, including AI technologies, as the company moves its design work onto digital models.
The company said digital models let its engineers analyze far larger volumes of data and test many more aircraft layouts before choosing the best one, which makes developing new modifications faster and cheaper over an aircraft’s life cycle. UAC added that it is taking a measured approach to AI and will only use the new tools where they make sense and help solve specific engineering problems.
“Digital technology makes it possible to take a larger sample and understand a problem more deeply. Over the life cycle, this will be faster and cheaper when creating the next modifications,” UAC specialists said.
The statement follows remarks by UAC general designer Sergey Korotkov, who said on Oct. 13 that there is no reason not to use AI in aircraft design as long as it helps with the task at hand and is applied thoughtfully. UAC has already been testing the idea, and in May its chief executive, Vadim Badekha, said the company was running a pilot project with Sberbank to use the bank’s GigaChat AI model for generative design of a new aircraft at the early design stage, with plans to extend it later to strength and aerodynamic calculations.
The shift to domestic digital tools has been driven largely by sanctions, since Western design software vendors such as Dassault Systèmes, Siemens and Autodesk pulled out of Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and left the country’s aerospace industry without the programs it had relied on for decades. UAC says it has since replaced software at its design bureaus with Russian products, equipping about 4,000 engineering workstations and swapping out nine key product lifecycle management modules, and on Oct. 16 it said digital design had cut some aircraft system calculations, such as cabin heat balance and hydraulic networks, from months to days.
Those efforts come as UAC struggles with delays on its most important civil programs, which have had to replace Western parts and systems with Russian-made equivalents. President Vladimir Putin said in June that the MC-21 had been set back by almost two years, partly because of problems with the wing, and First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said certification of the version built entirely with Russian components is now planned for the end of 2027.

articles.title: ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Andrew Roth
articles.body:
They say the first casualty of war is truth. For the Trump administration, the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.
Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”
In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.
And that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardian recently obtained a Russian strategy document showing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.
As Witkoff met Putin on Wednesday, schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border.
Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.
“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.
“And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.”
As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.
Those lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes for Ukraine to capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.
Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.
For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with Iskander-K missiles and 186 drones, air defences down 150 UAVs
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine with Iskander-K missiles and 186 drones, air defences down 150 UAVs
Russia attacked Ukraine with Iskander-K cruise missiles and 186 drones on the night of 20-21 October. Air defence forces have destroyed or jammed 150 UAVs, while another 10 remain airborne.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: The attack began at 18:00 on 20 October. Russian forces launched Iskander-K cruise missiles from the airspace over Rostov Oblast. The number of missiles launched and how many were intercepted have not been reported.
Russia also attacked Ukraine with 186 Shahed loitering munitions (88 jet-powered), Gerbera attack drones, S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T drone- and air-launched cruise missiles and Parodiya decoy UAVs.
The drones were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk, Chauda and Hvardiiske (Crimea).
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.
Quote: "As of 08:30, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 150 Shaheds (63 of which were jet-powered), S8000 Banderol/Dan-Ts, Gerberas and drones of other types. Another 10 attack drones remain airborne, combat work is ongoing!
Hits by aerial assets have been recorded at 27 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at 13 locations."
Background:
- Russian drones attacked Kyiv from the evening of 20 October and into the morning of 21 October.
- At around 07:00, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that a Russian drone had hit a 24-storey residential building in the Sviatoshynskyi district at the level of the 19th floor. A fire broke out.
- Parked cars caught fire in the Desnianskyi district after a drone crashed onto them. A drone strike on a transport infrastructure facility in the Solomianskyi district caused a fire and another drone was reported to have crashed in an open area.
